transcript: Mondrian thought paintings like this could help fix society. But...Paris wasn't buying it. Ya know, Actually buying it. It's 1921. His abstract paintings are a tough sell. So he paints flowers, too. Petals. Stems. A rose that looks like a rose. They help pay the bills. Then he goes back to this. Red. Blue. Black. Yellow. Gray. Put "Composition with" in front of that and you've got the title. Like a paint-store receipt. Look at that black block down at the bottom. The huge stretch of gray up on the right. Then the yellow. One little square, squeezed into the corner. Hardly any yellow at all. But your eye still goes there. Nothing matches. Somehow, it holds together. And Mondrian thinks that balance could work outside a painting. In buildings. Furniture. The way people live together. Which is a lot to put on a yellow square. But three years later, Gerrit Rietveld builds the Schröder House in the Netherlands. White walls. Black lines. Red, blue, yellow. It looks like a Mondrian you can walk into. Try that with a rose. Mondrian had been working on his own room, too. White walls. Colored rectangles he could move around. A friend remembered the trip up to his Paris studio. A horrible, shabby stairwell. Then you open the door. Her words: "As you stepped inside, you were in Paradise." He lived like that for fifteen years. He even kept a fake tulip. Painted its leaves white. He painted flowers Paris would buy. Then painted the green off the one he kept.

title: THREE WOMEN AT THE SPRING
transcript: Picasso spent the summer of 1921 painting these three women over and over. Same three women. Same setup. Move a hand. Shift a leg. Start again. And eventually he gets here. Nearly seven feet tall. Look at these women. Huge. Heavy. Built like Roman statues somebody rolled in off a temple. Big hands. Big feet. Everybody looks like they weigh a ton. And here's the strange part. At the exact same time, in the same garage studio, Picasso was painting Three Musicians. That loud, flat, chopped-up thing. Costumes. Color. Cubism. He was making them side by side. One painting looks like Picasso just blew painting apart. The other looks like he went back two thousand years. Same guy. Same summer. But come back to these three. Nobody's moving. The middle one leans her cheek into her hand. The woman on the right sits sideways, fingers resting on that big jug. Like they've got forever. Now look at the middle woman's other hand. Palm up. Held right underneath where you'd expect the spring to run. And nothing touches it. The spring just... doesn't show up where it should.

title: BALLET MÉCANIQUE
transcript: Sooner or later, a woman with a sack on her shoulder shows up. Watch her climb those stairs. And then… she's back at the bottom. Same woman. Same sack. Up she goes. Fernand Léger, one of the big painters in Paris, made this with an American filmmaker, Dudley Murphy. The only film Léger took on himself. It starts with Charlie Chaplin. Well, a cut-out of him. Lifts his hat. Disappears. The original title was Chaplin Presents the Mechanical Ballet. Then a woman on a swing. That's Murphy's wife. Then it's off. A whisk, all tangled wires. The wide mouth of a funnel. Light catching a copper pot. And at one point, in a shiny ball, you can catch the two men filming. They've ended up in their own movie. No plot. Léger figured painting had already stopped needing a story. Why couldn't film? Get a camera close enough to something ordinary, and it starts to have a personality. Then cut to something else. See what happens between them. This becomes one of the most influential experimental films ever made. And it was supposed to have music. George Antheil wrote it. Sixteen player pianos. Airplane propellers. A siren. Keeping sixteen player pianos together turns out to be a problem. So the film goes one way. The music goes another. In Paris, the music gets its own concert. There are accounts of fistfights out in the street. Over the music. Léger actually wrote down what he wanted to do to you. First, amaze you. Then make you uneasy. Then keep going until you can't take it anymore.

title: TWO CHILDREN ARE THREATENED BY A NIGHTINGALE
transcript: Okay, so. Start with the boy. It's the eighteen-nineties. Little German kid, caught measles, fever through the roof, stuck in bed for days. There's a panel on the wall, fake mahogany, printed wood grain, cheapest thing in the room. And the fever gets going, and the grain starts to move. An eye comes out of it. Then a nose. Then a bird's head. Kid lies there watching the wall turn into things. Never forgets it. His whole life, never forgets it. Thirty years later, that kid is Max Ernst. He builds this thing. Look at it. It's not even a painting really, it's a little stage. A box. And inside the box, total emergency. Girl flat out in the grass. Other girl swinging a knife. A guy up on the roof with a child under his arm, grabbing for that knob like it's the emergency exit. So okay. Where's the danger. What's everybody running from. Look for it. It's the bird. That little thing floating up there. A nightingale. A songbird. The title even says it right out: Two Children Are Threatened by a Nightingale. The most harmless creature on earth, that's what he picks. That's the joke. And nobody inside the box is laughing. And then, and this is the part, look at the gate down in front. Real wood. Nailed on. The little house, real. The knob, actual knob, sticking out at you. The dream is not staying inside the frame. It's coming through. Fever logic, that's what this is. Sky's calm. Grass is bright. Panic's total. But the cause? Nothing. Which, be honest, is what dread actually is. Your brain going, something is wrong here. And refusing to tell you what.

title: HOUSE BY THE RAILROAD
transcript: You know this house. Look at it a second. Tall, gray, fancy roof, windows staring down at you. You've seen it before, at the movies. It's the Psycho house. And no, that's not a stretch. Hitchcock said it. The Bates mansion came from looking at this painting. Hopper found out and loved it. The screenwriter topped it. Said Norman Bates, if the guy were a painting, he'd be a Hopper. Okay, but now the weird part. Look for the scary thing. There isn't one. Broad daylight. Blue sky. No ghost, no shadow, nothing wrong you can point at. Just this big proud Victorian standing up straight, and train tracks slicing right across the front of it. Like somebody crossed it out. And that's the whole story right there. Quietly brutal. This used to be the house. The fancy one. The one people slowed down to look at. Then the railroad came through, and the world went with it. Nobody tore the house down. Nobody had to. It just got left. And maybe Hopper knew the feeling. Guy could barely sell a painting till he was past forty. And get this. When MoMA started collecting, the first painting in the door, painting number one, was this one. A whole museum dedicated to the new, and entry number one is the thing the new left behind. And the actual house? Still up there. Haverstraw, New York, right by the tracks.

title: THE BIRTH OF THE WORLD
transcript: First thing, this one is big. Eight feet tall, and most of it is fog. Stains, spills, washes of gray. Up close it barely looks decided. More like weather than a picture. That's the recipe, though. Miró primed the canvas badly on purpose, patchy, so the paint would never behave. Then he poured it, brushed it, flung it. Some of it soaks in, some of it sits there. Chance gets to paint the background. And then, this is the move, he comes back with a steady hand and drops in the little signs. A red balloon on a long yellow string. A black triangle that might be a kite. A white ball. Down in the corner, a spidery little star. His own description says it all. A sort of genesis, he called it. And then, his words, the second stage is carefully calculated. First the fog, then the thought. He didn't even name the thing. His friends were poets, Surrealist poets, and they took one look and called it The Birth of the World. Poets, right? But maybe that's why it stuck. It has that look, the second before things click. And pouring paint, letting the mess lead? That's Pollock's whole legend, twenty years later. Miró got there first, on a farm in Catalonia, with nobody watching. And that's sort of how everything starts, isn't it. Spills. Nobody knowing what they're doing. Then someone draws one line with confidence, and everyone acts like the plan was always there. Anyway. Maybe he just caught the world early. While it was still deciding what it wanted to be.

title: WASSILY CHAIR
transcript: Okay, quick inventory. Cushions? Nope. Padding? Nope. Wood? Nope. A few bent steel tubes, some straps of black cloth, and you can see straight through the whole thing. And somehow you still know exactly what it is. A club chair. Built for cigars and long afternoons. He kept the idea and basically threw out the chair. Marcel Breuer is twenty-three when he designs this, and his actual job at the Bauhaus is running the woodshop. So he's the guy in charge of the trees! Then he buys a bicycle and can't stop staring at the handlebars. Steel tube. Light, strong, bent by a machine, every one identical. He's thinking: If steel can hold a man at full speed on cobblestones, a living room should be easy. So this is an armchair drawn in air. Look where you actually sit. Not on the steel. On cloth, pulled tight, hanging in the middle of it. The metal never touches you. He bragged about it the only way he knew how. Called it his most extreme work, "the least artistic, the most logical, the least cozy, the most mechanical." A man in love, talking like a parts catalog. The name came later, and not from him. Kandinsky taught down the hall, loved it, got a copy made for his place. Forty years later an Italian company hears that story and starts calling it the Wassily. The painter didn't design a bolt of it. A year later Breuer prints a little film strip in the Bauhaus magazine. His chairs, year by year, less material every time. The last frame is a woman sitting on nothing at all. Eventually, he says, we'll sit on columns of air. So even Breuer didn't think this was the future. Just one more frame. The plan was for the chair to keep disappearing, and this is as far as it got.

title: THE FOUNTAINS
transcript: So where's the light coming from in this one? The big sun in the back? The glowing ball at the bottom? That white thing climbing the middle? Everything's just lit, all of it, off everything else, the whole thing rising slow, humming. File it under wind chimes. Guru things, crystals. Then stand here a minute, and apologize. Now, the story. This was painted inside a windmill. Seriously, a real one, out on Long Island. Agnes Pelton lived in it, alone, paying her rent by painting portraits of the rich summer crowd. Nice dresses, checks clearing. Then in 1926, in her mid-forties, she starts making these. Not what's out the window. What she sees with her eyes closed. This is one of the first ones she ever did. Meanwhile in Paris, everybody's breaking guitars into little cubes. And she's in a windmill, painting light. And the quiet runs in the family. Her grandmother was Elizabeth Tilton. Her affair with Henry Ward Beecher, the most famous preacher in America, was the biggest scandal of the eighteen-hundreds. Six months in court, every paper in the country, and he walks. The family's wrecked. Agnes's mother more or less goes into hiding, runs a little music school in Brooklyn, raises her daughter in a house where nobody talks loud. So look what that turned into. The loudest noise in America happens to this family, and the kid grows up making the quietest pictures in the building. No faces. No story. Just light, minding its own business. She painted like this for thirty-five more years. Alone mostly, unsold mostly, completely unbothered. So yeah, you can stop looking for the light source. It was never in the picture.

title: ABSTRACTION BLUE
transcript: So, she mails the drawings to a friend in New York. Then... she gets scared. She’s twenty-seven, teaching art at a little college in South Carolina. She’s put aside everything she was taught and started making shapes in charcoal. She writes to her friend that she’s scared nobody will get them. And scared somebody actually will. Anyway, find that white line. The friend takes the drawings to Alfred Stieglitz, a photographer who runs a gallery. Then Stieglitz just hangs them up without asking. O’Keeffe eventually finds out and tells him to take them down. But he won’t. That show gets her career going. Everything you know her for comes later. Flowers, cow skulls, the desert. Dorm posters. Stieglitz falls for her. Photographs her. Shows the photographs, including a bunch of nudes. And with Freud the hot new thing, suddenly every art critic’s a doctor. O’Keeffe complains they’ve turned her into some unearthly creature floating around in the air. Then she paints the big flowers, and the critics see sex. She paints more flowers. More sex. She could’ve painted a filing cabinet. They’d have found something. But through all this, she keeps making abstract pictures too. And right in the middle of the flowers, she makes this. Come back to the white line. It’s wide at the top, then thins almost to a hair. On the left, a minty green shape, cupped in dark blue. On the right, almost its other half, only grayer. Like somebody cut it down the middle and put it back a little off. She once said shapes and colors could say things she had no words for. Look where the two curves meet the white line. They almost line up. Almost.

title: THE MENACED ASSASSIN
transcript: He killed her. That part of the case is settled. The woman on the couch, the blood at her mouth, the man standing right there in the room. His coat and hat are already waiting on the chair. And instead of running, he's bent over the gramophone, playing a record. He stayed for the music. Now look at what he can't see. Two men in bowler hats flanking the doorway he has to walk through, one holding a club, the other holding a net. A fucking net. Like they're collecting a butterfly. And in the window behind him, three identical faces lined up over the balcony rail, watching. Nobody in this painting moves. The record just keeps going. Magritte was twenty-eight and completely drunk on crime pulp. Fantômas, the French serials, the silent films. The two men at the door are staged exactly like a shot from a 1913 Fantômas movie. He storyboarded a painting. One frame, paused right before everything happens, and you never get the next one. Now the title. The Menaced Assassin. Not the murdered woman. The assassin, menaced. The title walks straight past the victim and starts worrying about the killer. He's the one in danger here, the painting says. And be honest, you've gone along with it. You've been checking his escape route. Clocking the club, the net, the three guys at the window. Somewhere in the last minute you quietly joined his side. And the record's almost over.

title: THE LOVERS
transcript: Look at them. They're kissing. Neither one's taking the cloth off. Both heads wrapped. Lips pressed through fabric. Hers hangs loose. His is pulled tight around the throat. Right over the collar and tie. Dressed for the occasion, apparently. And they're not stopping. Gray room. One brown wall. Painted neat and flat, like there's nothing odd going on. That's Magritte. The Belgian Surrealist who dressed like a bank clerk. Paints everything exactly how it looks. Then gets one thing wrong. Your brain's already gone: couple kissing. Got it. Then you notice the cloth. They're pressed right up against each other. Still can't get to each other. That's his big subject. Wanting what you can't reach. He painted lovers four times that year. Twice with the cloth. These two kiss. The other two just stand there, side by side. Like a wedding photo. Except nobody's got a face. So, there's a story that follows this painting around. When Magritte was thirteen, his mother drowned herself in the river Sambre. The story goes that he was there when they pulled her out. And her nightgown was wrapped around her face. His friend Louis Scutenaire wrote it down in 1947. And you hear that and think: well, there it is. The cloth. The hidden faces. Except somebody eventually checks. This guy David Sylvester, an art historian. Goes through the old newspapers and police records. Turns out they found her seventeen days after she disappeared. A kilometer downstream. Sylvester says the familiar story doesn't hold up. So what did the boy actually see? What did somebody tell him? Harder to say. And Magritte wasn't much help with people trying to explain his paintings. He said they concealed nothing. They evoked mystery. And mystery was unknowable. Which isn't quite the same as saying: here's a thing that happened to me, and here's a picture of it. His mother died in 1912. He painted this in 1928. You can see why people put the two together. That would explain it. But it doesn't mean it does.

title: THE MOON
transcript: This painting is so simple it feels like a dare. Five things. A yellow moon. Some clouds. Green hills. A stream. A cactus. You could draw it from memory after seeing it once. Now look at the cactus again. The shape of it. A round little body, a head, something like an arm. It's standing at the edge of the water the way a person stands at a railing, looking up at the moon. She didn't put a figure in the landscape. She grew one out of the ground. Tarsila do Amaral spent years in Paris learning the rules. Léger, Gleizes, the whole cubist apparatus. She called it her military service. Service ends. She goes home to Brazil, and she takes the weapons with her. And 1928 is the year it all detonates. She paints another canvas, Abaporu, as a birthday present for her husband. The name is two Tupi-Guarani words: the man who eats human flesh. Her husband takes one look and writes a manifesto around it. The idea: Brazil shouldn't imitate European culture. It should eat it. Digest it. Turn it into something that could only come from here. That manifesto became a whole movement. Abaporu is the loud version. The Moon is the quiet one. Same year, same hand, same cactus. Tarsila is about as famous as a painter can be in Brazil. And this museum didn't own a single thing she made until 2019. This was the first. The dare sat there for ninety years before this building took it.

title: BIRD IN SPACE
transcript: So...a crate from Paris lands at New York customs, and the officers pry it open. Inside, packed in straw, four and a half feet of polished bronze. Narrow, curved, coming to a point. The paperwork says it's a sculpture called Bird in Space. Now, art enters America duty-free. But these guys look in the crate and see no wings, no feathers, no beak. No bird. Just a gold spike. So a customs man, a real man with a real stamp, rules that this is not art. He files it, and this is real, under Kitchen Utensils and Hospital Supplies. A Brancusi. In with the soup ladles and the bedpans. Then they bill the owner forty percent, like it's a shipment of forks. The owner is Edward Steichen, maybe the most famous photographer alive. He does the most American thing possible. He sues. So now it's Brancusi versus the United States, an actual federal case, where lawyers put sculptors on the stand and ask them, under oath, to define a bird. The dumbest question of the century, and the whole future of art riding on it. But the question was the point. Brancusi spent decades on birds, taking something away every time. Feathers, gone. Feet, gone. Finally the bird, gone. What's left is the lift. He wasn't carving a bird. He was carving what a bird does. The law said sculpture had to imitate a natural object. This imitates nothing. On purpose. The crime was the achievement. Two years later, the court folds. There's a new school of art, the judge writes, it deals in ideas instead of copies, and like it or not, it exists. From a federal bench, that's practically poetry. We don't get it. It counts anyway. The bird from the trial has a brother. You're looking at it. Cast the same year as the verdict. Same bronze, same curve. Filed under sculpture this time. Still doing the only thing it ever wanted. Going up.

title: SOW
transcript: Paris. A studio, furniture shoved against the wall. Five suitcases, open on the floor. The gramophone starts. The lights go down. A grown man gets on his knees. Wire acrobats. A knife-thrower. A lion. Wire, cork, string, thread, and pulleys. Calder works them all by hand. Does the noises. Does the voices. He's dead serious through all of it. The whole thing can run two hours. With rent due, he buys planks, swipes boxes, makes bleachers, and charges thirty people a night. Miró came to one of the Paris shows. Léger was there too. “I liked the bits of paper best,” Miró said. Little weighted scraps of white paper, fluttering down a wire onto a performer’s shoulder. That little trapeze really works. The man running it had a degree in mechanical engineering. While building the circus, Calder starts making animals that don’t need him at all. Like this one. Made in 1928. Seventeen inches long, bent out of steel wire. One line for the back. A curl for the tail. A coil for the eye. Along the belly, a zigzag of loops. That’s the udder. That’s where the title comes from. How little can you use and still get a whole animal? You can see straight through it. Half of it is air caught inside the wire. By then, the French were calling Calder le roi du fil de fer. The king of wire. Fifteen years later, he opens the suitcases again. Here at MoMA for his retrospective. Two nights, for friends and staff. Same man. Same knees. Same wire. Calder had made a wire donkey too. MoMA’s checklist puts the two together. “Sow.” Then “Ass.” After the show, Calder gives this one to the museum. The circus moves on. But she stays.

title: THE TREACHERY OF IMAGES
transcript: A Belgian guy paints a pipe. Look at the pipe. It's really well painted. The kind you'd see in a catalog, right above "Makes a great gift for Dad." Then underneath it, he writes: Ceci n'est pas une pipe. This is not a pipe. Foucault wrote a book about it. Undergrads cite it at parties. It's been called one of the most important artworks of the twentieth century. Magritte would have found all of that very silly. He thought the answer was obvious. First, that pipe. The reason it's painted like a catalog illustration is that Magritte used to do catalog illustrations. Before he was Magritte, he worked in advertising. Wallpaper, cigar posters. For years. This is just what he knew how to paint. Now see how careful the script is? Like a kid doing his handwriting homework? That's because it's copied from French primary-school reading books. Picture on top, sentence below. Voici un chien. Here is a dog. Voici une pipe. Here is a pipe. Magritte grew up on those books. He took the exact layout and blew it up. So what you're looking at is an ad. And a children's book. Two formats that have been confidently telling you what stuff is for your entire life. And this one is correcting itself. Magritte's explanation, when a reporter finally pinned him down: "Could you stuff my pipe? No. It's a representation, is it not? So if I had written 'This IS a pipe,' I'd have been lying." That's the whole painting. He smoked a pipe. He painted a pipe. He pointed out, for the record, that the painting is not, in fact, a pipe. You can't smoke it. It's a rectangle of pigment. That's all he meant. Everyone else built a philosophy department around it. Magritte was in a three-piece suit, in his dining room in Brussels, commuting from his bedroom to his easel. While the world fought over what he meant, he just kept going. Little joke. Little joke. Little joke.

title: THE FALSE MIRROR
transcript: So you came here to look at it, and it's looking at you. One enormous eye. And where the iris should be, sky. Blue, daylight, clouds drifting through. And dead center, the pupil, a flat black circle. There's no glint in it. Painted eyes usually get that little spark to show the reflection of the room they're looking at. This one gives nothing back. So which way does it go? Are you looking through the eye, at the sky on the other side? Or into it, at what it sees? Magritte, the Belgian Surrealist, called it The False Mirror, which answers nothing. That was the idea. Anyway, Man Ray owned this one for a while in the thirties, before it ended up here. In 1951, CBS needed a logo. Their creative director came up with an eye. He said he got it from Shaker folk art. People have been pointing at this painting anyway. The CBS eye. It's been staring out of TV sets ever since. One eye sells. And one watches.

title: BARCELONA CHAIR
transcript: Picture it. Barcelona, 1929, a world's fair. Germany's pavilion is the strangest building anybody's ever seen. Marble walls, a floating roof, a shallow pool, and almost nothing inside. And the King and Queen of Spain are coming to open it. You can't hand a king a folding stool. So the architect designs them a throne. Two, actually. Gleaming steel X-frames, white leather. No carving, no gold, no crown anywhere on it. And the X is doing the work. It's the oldest power-seat shape there is. Roman magistrates sat on X-frame chairs two thousand years ago. Mies van der Rohe just stripped off the costume and chromed the bones. Alright, so it's opening day. The king and queen walk through, look around, and leave. Neither one ever sits down. Two thrones, built for exactly two people on earth, and those two people walk right past. The chairs got stood up. A year later the whole pavilion gets torn down with the rest of the fair. The chairs survive. Then it gets strange. The throne no king ever sat in takes over the world. Every corporate lobby, every law firm, every waiting room with ambitions. You've probably sat on this throne yourself, holding a coffee, waiting for somebody to call you in. And there's one more name in this story. Lilly Reich. Mies's collaborator, maybe the lead, depending who you ask. Her name fell off this chair for most of a century. So the king never sat, the building came down, the credit got lost. The chair's still here. Less is more, the man liked to say.

title: COMPOSITION NO. II, WITH RED AND BLUE
transcript: Okay, so for a lot of people, Mondrian is a dress. You know the one. Yves Saint Laurent takes the black lines, the red, the blue, the white, and puts armholes in it. Huge hit. Copied everywhere. Years later, once he's collecting Mondrians himself, Saint Laurent says: "Mondrian is purity, and you can't go any further in painting." Which sounds like fashion talk until you get to Mondrian. Take this one. Composition No. II, with Red and Blue. Not quite sixteen inches tall. The thing is, is that Mondrian belonged to the Dutch Theosophical Society. Part religion. Part philosophy. Part attempt to explain the invisible order underneath everything. And he didn't just dabble. He joined in Holland. Decades later, when he moved to London, he had his membership transferred. Ok so we got New country. New studio. War closing in. And somewhere in the paperwork: Transfer the Theosophy membership. Check. By New York, he's no longer active in the Society. Never quits. He dies a member. In a letter, he puts it pretty plainly. "I got everything from The Secret Doctrine." Everything. That's a funny word from a man who puts almost nothing on a canvas. Four black lines. Red at the top left. Blue on the right. Mostly white. That's the whole cast. But look at where the lines stop. The one along the bottom runs into the upright and quits. So the white at the bottom right has nothing under it. It just walks off the edge. It looks inevitable now. It wasn't. Somebody had to decide exactly where every line stopped. Now get close to the bottom left. Inside the black bar, in red: P M. Then 25. Except he painted this in 1929. Part of the original date had disappeared. Mondrian restored it himself. Except, wrong year. Space, he had under control. Time was another matter.

title: FISH
transcript: Six feet of grey marble balanced on a white pedestal. Brancusi called it Fish. Okay. But look at the stone. Those white streaks run the length of it, like water rushing past. He didn't paint those on. They were in the marble. He cut straight into the stone himself. The usual way back then was a clay model, and hired carvers to copy it. He called his way "the true road to sculpture." Brancusi told another sculptor, Malvina Hoffman, that when you see a fish, you don't think about its scales. You see it flash through the water. He said he wanted "just the flash of its spirit." He made seven fish. This was the last one, and the biggest. From the side, you get all six feet of it. From the narrow end, almost nothing. One step to the side and it changes again. That's a good trick for a slab of rock. But there's another one. That little support under the marble? It's a pivot. While he talked to Hoffman, he gave it a push. The fish used to spin.

title: THE PERSISTENCE OF MEMORY
transcript: Okay, so you walk up to this one expecting a wall. You've seen it a thousand times. Posters, mugs, the works. And up close? Tiny. Barely bigger than a sheet of paper. The most recognizable clocks on the planet, and the whole thing would fit in a folder. Look at what's happening. Time's melting. Not smashed, not broken, the watches have just gone soft. Like they sat out in the sun too long. One's hanging off a dead branch. One's sliding off the table. And where'd it come from? The way Dalí told it, he's home with a headache, Gala's gone to the movies, and he's sitting after dinner staring at a painting he can't finish. There's a hunk of camembert on the table, going soft. He looks at the cheese. Looks at the painting. Two hours later, melting clocks. For years everybody wanted it to be about Einstein. Relativity, time bending. A scientist actually wrote to ask him. Dalí said nope. It was the cheese. It's not just the clocks. That orange one in the corner that kept its shape? Crawling with ants. Dalí painted ants when he meant something's rotting. And that pale lumpy thing in the middle, the shut eye, the long lashes? People say that's him. His own face, flopped on the ground, melting too. So everything's coming apart. Time, the watch, the man who painted it. Everything. Except one thing. Look past all of it, to the back. Those cliffs. Sharp, solid, not melting at all. And that's no made-up nowhere. That's his backyard, the coast he grew up on, in Catalonia. The whole world here turns to liquid, and the one thing he paints hard as a rock is home. He called it The Persistence of Memory. So the clocks don't last. He doesn't last. Time goes soft. But home? It stays put.

title: AGRARIAN LEADER ZAPATA
transcript: Okay, look at that horse first. Big, white, gorgeous. And it's not even Mexican. Rivera basically lifts it from an Italian battle painting from the 1400s, by a guy named Uccello. A rich nobleman's horse. And look who he hands it to. That guy in sandals. That's Zapata. He led peasants in the Mexican Revolution, fighting to take land back from the wealthy estates and return it to the people working it. Tierra y libertad. Land and liberty. And look at how Rivera paints him. Not the badass with the bullet belts and giant sombrero from the photographs. Nah. Quiet. On foot. And what's he holding? A machete. The thing you cut sugarcane with. Everybody behind him has grabbed whatever was around. A sickle. A bow. Some hoes. It's an army of garden tools. Now look down by his feet. That's the loser. A wealthy hacienda owner, face-down in his fancy riding boots, one gloved hand flopped against Zapata's bare foot. That white horse was his. Zapata took it off him. Rivera took it off Uccello. Same move, twice. Now, this thing is fresco. Michelangelo. The Sistine Chapel. About the least portable art form imaginable. Rivera makes one with no wall. A huge slab built to travel. So he packs it up, and wheels the revolution directly into the Museum of Modern Art. At this point MoMA is barely two years old, and a museum co-founded by Abby Rockefeller gives an outspoken Communist its galleries. Rivera uses the fanciest medium imaginable to turn a peasant revolutionary into a saint. The place is mobbed. Two years later, the Rockefellers give him a wall at Rockefeller Center. He paints Lenin into it. They smash it off with hammers. But not this one. Same Communist. Same revolution. Still hanging. They smashed the loud one. They kept the dangerous one.

title: GIRL BEFORE A MIRROR
transcript: So Marie-Thérèse Walter is seventeen, out shopping for a collar, when a random guy walks up and takes her by the arm. Says she has an interesting face. That they’re going to do great things together. And then he says, “I’m Picasso.” This means nothing to her. She just notices his tie. Red and black. So he shows her a book about himself, in Chinese or Japanese. He thought that was funny. You couldn’t read his name on it. He’s forty-five. Married, with a child at home. For years, he keeps her secret. Even works her initials, M and T, into paintings of guitars, where his wife won’t notice them. Five years later, he’s fifty, with a chauffeur, a château, and a huge Paris retrospective coming up. He thinks this show will decide whether he still matters. All winter and spring, he paints Marie-Thérèse. He said this was the one he liked best. Didn’t say why. Look at her face. That lilac profile on one side, and the hot yellow face looking straight out on the other. Then follow her arm across the mirror’s post. The woman in the reflection looks darker. Heavier. Picasso never explained her. Other people have. Maybe the girl’s older self. Her shadow. Paintings of a girl at a mirror used to carry a little warning. The face doesn’t last. Anyway, that June, the retrospective opens. Portraits of his wife and son get the place of honor. But Marie-Thérèse’s face is all through the recent paintings. Picasso doesn’t go to the opening. He goes to the movies instead. Later, MoMA’s director chooses this for the museum. Calls it the finest Picasso in ten years. Decades later, they X-ray it. Turns out under those stripes down her side, she started out with her back to you. Picasso painted over her fast. Black lines and house paint.

title: THE PALACE AT 4 A.M.
transcript: It fits on a table. Which is almost funny, because look at the title: The Palace at 4 A.M. Sounds huge. Marble, servants, somebody crying on a balcony. And it's this. A rickety little cage of wood and wire and string, two feet tall, no walls. More like a stage set nobody finished. So Giacometti is in his early thirties, falls hard for a woman. Six months, completely gone. And the way he tells it, the two of them built a palace together at night. Out of matchsticks. Somebody would move wrong and a whole wing would collapse. Build it, knock it down, build it again. Then it ends. She's gone. And he builds the palace for real. Now, careful. He barely explained any of this. Said these objects appeared in his head already finished, and he built them without asking what they meant. Most of what you hear is guesswork. But he did identify two pieces. That stiff little figure on the left? His mother, the way he remembered her from childhood. Long dark dress. And that pale shape hanging in the middle? That's him. So his mother's in there. He's in there. But the woman, the reason the palace exists, he never identifies. Then look right. That run of vertebrae trapped in the cage. You can see why everybody decides that's her. The one person he couldn't name. Reduced to a spine in a box. He built the palace in matchsticks and watched it fall apart. So he made it once more in wood and wire, where it couldn't. The relationship didn't last. But this little palace has been standing for almost a hundred years.

title: BEHIND THE GARE SAINT-LAZARE
transcript: So here's Cartier-Bresson in Paris, 1932, standing behind Saint-Lazare Station. The ground's torn up, there's a giant puddle on the other side of a fence, and he can't see a thing. So he takes this little Leica, shoves it through a gap in the boards, and clicks. That's it. No looking through the camera. No lining anything up. Basically a guess. And this is what he gets. A man floating over the water, one heel about to come down. Underneath him, a perfect reflection doing the same jump upside down. And behind him, on the wall, a poster of a dancer with her leg kicked out in almost exactly the same pose. Three people jumping at once. The man, his reflection, the dancer. Cartier-Bresson had no idea. He found all of that later, when he saw the photograph. Which is funny, because this picture goes on to become Exhibit A for his whole theory of photography. Cartier-Bresson believed there was this tiny fraction of a second when everything suddenly came together. What was happening, what it meant, and the shape it made in the frame. For one instant, life organized itself. You saw it, you clicked. Miss it, gone. They called it the decisive moment. And photographers have been stalking puddles ever since. Except Cartier-Bresson never called it that. His book had a much scruffier French title, Images à la sauvette. Pictures grabbed on the run. The Americans gave it the big dramatic name. So one of the most famous examples of the photographer seeing the perfect instant? He didn't see it. He stuck his camera through a fence and got lucky. And maybe that's why the picture is so good. The man hasn't landed. The reflection hasn't broken. For one more split second, he's still floating there, and anything could happen.

title: BIRD-HEAD
transcript: This one's got a face. Big flat square head, two round eyes, a beak where the nose should be, little stubby legs. Looks friendly. Looks completely ridiculous. Like something a kid would draw if you said, draw a bird, but also make him a paper bag guy thing. Hold that thought, because there's a reason. Max Ernst is fifteen. His pet cockatoo dies in the night. And that same night, near enough, his baby sister is born. Now follow the teenage logic here. Bird gone. Baby arrives. Same house, same night. So clearly, the bird turned into the baby. That's not how anything works. Doesn't matter. The idea goes in deep and never comes out. He blamed the baby, by the way. His own sister. For the bird. And he wrote all of this down himself, as a grown man, completely straight-faced. And it gets better. Years later he invents an alter ego. A bird, obviously. Loplop. Official title: the Bird Superior. Superior to whom? To him. To Ernst. His own imaginary bird outranked him. And Loplop is everywhere in his work, presenting pictures, presiding over things, a feathered master of ceremonies. So. The bronze. Square head, round eyes, beak. A bird trying to be a face, or a face trying to be a bird, depending on the day. Maybe it's Loplop, holding still for once. Or the closest thing to a self-portrait the man ever made. He spent his whole life half-convinced he was part bird. This might be the honest passport photo.

title: THE PORTRAIT
transcript: Dinner is served. Ham, a bottle of wine, an empty glass. Knife and fork lined up straight. Everything clean and polite, painted like a page from a cookbook. Except the ham is looking at you. One eye, dead center, wide open. You're in a staring contest with your lunch, and you're going to lose. So what does the eye mean? Careful. Magritte hated this question. He hated symbols. Hated being decoded. You weren't supposed to solve the mystery. You were supposed to stand there and let it bother you. People guess anyway. Maybe it's the animal getting one last look at whoever ordered it. Maybe it's your conscience, served cold. Maybe the title is the clue. Magritte called this The Portrait, not Still Life, and a portrait is supposed to look back. Pick one. He'd have hated it. Try another. He'd have hated that one too. He was very fair that way. But the painting did eventually give up one secret. Just not the one anybody was looking for. In 2013, MoMA put it under an X-ray and found another painting underneath. It was part of The Enchanted Pose, a canvas Magritte had painted in 1927: two identical nude women standing side by side in an empty room. He was broke. He cut the canvas into four pieces and painted something new on top of each one. The other pieces turned up beneath paintings in Stockholm, Norwich, and Brussels. The last one wasn't found until 2017. So beneath the ham, the wine, and that one unblinking eye, there's part of a naked woman who disappeared for over eighty years.

title: THE OBJECT
transcript: Alright, here's the story Oppenheim used to tell. She's twenty-two, sitting at a café with Picasso and the photographer Dora Maar. On her wrist is a bracelet she designed, a brass cuff covered in fur. Picasso looks at it and says, basically, you could cover anything in fur. Oppenheim looks down at the table. Even this cup and saucer. Then she calls to the waiter, "A little more fur." That could have been it. Just a good line over coffee. But not long after, the Surrealists ask her to make something for a show. She remembers the joke, buys a plain white cup, saucer, and spoon, and covers the whole thing in fur. Your eyes understand it immediately. Cup. Saucer. Spoon. Then your mouth gets involved. Because the fur goes right up to the rim. You can already feel the wet hair against your lips. Your body makes the decision for you. Nope. That's the whole thing. She takes three objects designed to make drinking tea easy and civilized, and makes them impossible to use. People went nuts for it. André Breton, the writer and self-appointed leader of the Surrealist movement, gave it the grander title Luncheon in Fur. MoMA showed it and bought it that same year. The first work by a woman the museum ever owned. Great for the cup. A little rough on Oppenheim. Because after this, everyone wanted more fur. More shock. Another perfect Surrealist object. She spent years trying not to be reduced to the woman who made the furry teacup. Imagine making one joke at twenty-two and having everyone ask you to tell it again for the next fifty years. Still, look at it. Soft. Cozy. Then you picture it inside your mouth.

title: MIGRANT MOTHER
transcript: Her name was Florence Owens Thompson. For forty years, almost nobody knew that. March, 1936. Dorothea Lange's been on the road a month, shooting the Depression for a government program. She's tired, headed home, and she drives right past a sign by the road. Pea-pickers' camp. She goes another twenty miles before she gives up arguing with herself, turns the car around, and drives back. The pea crop's frozen. No work, no money, families just stranded there. Lange walks up to one tent. A woman, thirty-two, kids folded around her. Ten minutes, a few frames, moving in closer each time. And she never asked the woman her name. Never got her story. Then she got back in her car. This is the last frame. Look at her. The hand at the jaw. Two kids turned into her shoulders, hiding from the lens. A baby asleep in her lap. Everyone reads that look as despair. But despair gives up, and she hasn't. She's still running the math. Food, kids, tomorrow, and no version of it that comes out right. Then the picture runs in the papers. And within days, the government rushes twenty thousand pounds of food to that camp. One face moved all of that. But by the time it arrived, Thompson and her kids had already moved on down the road. They got none of it. No money. No credit. Not for decades. When a reporter finally found her in the seventies, she said she wished the picture had never been taken. That she'd been used. The photo doesn't tell you this part. She was Cherokee. Born in Oklahoma, full-blooded. America made a Native woman the face of the white Dust Bowl, and nobody asked her about that either.

title: MY GRANDPARENTS, MY PARENTS, AND I
transcript: It's painted on a sheet of zinc. Not canvas. Metal. About the size of a record sleeve. That's how Mexican retablos were made. You come through something bad. The fever breaks. The truck misses you. So you paint the disaster. You paint the saint who pulled you out. Then you hang it in a church. Ya know. Thank you, cause I'm still here. Frida and Diego Rivera collected hundreds of them. This isn't one exactly. No saint. No miracle. But she borrows the metal and the scale for a family tree. So here's what she puts on it. Four grandparents up in the sky. Her mother's family over Mexico on the left. Her father's family over the Atlantic on the right. Her parents in the middle, traced from their wedding photograph. Her mother's hand still resting on her father's shoulder. Exactly where the photographer left it. And one red ribbon running through all of them. It forks twice at the top. Below that, one line. Down from the left. Behind her parents. Along the bottom. Back up the other side. Frida is at the low point. A naked kid in the courtyard, holding the loop. She's too big for her own house, which she's drawn flat, from above, like a floor plan. Blue walls. On her mother's dress, a fetus. Down in the dirt by the cactus, an egg with sperm coming at it. Her own conception, squeezed into the family tree. This is 1936. A year earlier, Nazi Germany passed the Nuremberg Race Laws. Now a family tree could be used against you. List your grandparents. Prove your blood. She makes one too. But Frida had a loose relationship with official records. She liked to say her father was a Hungarian Jew. He wasn't. He was a German Lutheran, a jeweler's son from Pforzheim. She says she was born in 1910, the year the Mexican Revolution began. She wasn't. She was already three. Her official birth certificate said 1907.

title: COMPOSITION IN WHITE, BLACK, AND RED
transcript: So we got one red bar. That's all the color he gives you. Along the bottom edge. Thin. Stubborn. Just above it, small, in red: P M 36. Even his signature stays within the budget. Everything else is white and black. More than three feet of canvas. Not much on it. But look at what that little red bar has to balance. All that white. He's not making the two sides match. He's trying to make things that don't match hold together. This is Mondrian's Composition in White, Black, and Red. Paris, 1936. And he thought paintings like this were temporary. Art gave you the harmony life couldn't. Yet, once that harmony got into the way people actually lived, art would have done its job. You wouldn't need a painting of it. You'd be living in it. In 1936, George Morris buys this directly from Mondrian for the Museum of Modern Art. MoMA is seven years old. Still deciding what modern art is. A year later, Nazi Germany gives its answer. They called it Degenerate. That summer, in Munich, the Nazis put confiscated art on display. Crowded rooms. Insults on the walls. The whole thing is designed so you point and laugh. Mondrians are seized from a museum in Hanover. But getting rid of them doesn't always mean destroying them. Some are worth money abroad. Apparently, Degenerates travel well. One of those paintings is called Painting No. 2. Not the one in front of you. An earlier Mondrian. The Nazis hand it to a dealer to sell for foreign currency. A June 1939 letter says the New York dealer sent it back. Said it was "Damaged in transit." After that, nothing. So, Mondrian imagined a world so harmonious that paintings could disappear. But turns out the paintings started disappearing first.

title: GIBRALTAR
transcript: So, a wood so heavy it sinks. It’s called lignum vitae. Drop a block in a bucket and it goes straight to the bottom. That’s the lump underneath this thing. Split, pitted, looking like nobody’s touched it. Except for that dark surface down low. Somebody’s been at that. Then a piece of polished walnut cuts across it on a slant, smooth as a spoon. There’s a white ball at the low end, a red one up on a thin rod, and way up top, a little wooden crescent. Almost like a rock with a bit of sky over it. This is Calder. The mobile guy. The man who got sculpture moving, working here with a wood that won’t even float. The year he makes this, he has a show in New York. There’s a pencil sheet listing the works, each one a little doodle with a number and a price. This one’s number twenty-one. A scribbled peak with that slanted plate across it. Two hundred. No name yet. That same year, a dealer puts Calder in a book on Surrealism. But he can’t quite place him. Sometimes Surrealist, sometimes abstract. He wants Calder to pick a side. Calder’s got rough wood and polished walnut in the same piece. Look where they meet. The rough stuff comes up from underneath and pokes out above that smooth plate. A sculptor friend had already called the ones that don’t move “stabiles.” It’s a dig, but Calder kept the word. This is one. He later says names are tags. If he had to talk about a piece, he’d just make a little drawing. Number twenty-one does get a tag eventually. Gibraltar. As in the rock. This museum’s own catalogue lists it: Gibraltar. Stabile.

title: GUERNICA (TAPESTRY)
transcript: Okay, so picture this. You're walking down a hallway at the United Nations. Carpet. Fluorescent lights. Diplomats going back and forth with folders under their arms, everybody in a hurry. And on the wall, twenty-two feet across, somebody is screaming. It's Guernica. Well, sort of. Not the painting. A tapestry. Nelson Rockefeller commissioned it in the fifties. So now the most famous anti-war image in the world is made out of wool. Soft. Quiet. The kind of thing that absorbs sound. Picasso supervised that personally. They hang it right outside the room where the Security Council argues about war for a living. Airspace. Targets. Ceasefires. Sanctions. Whatever the crisis is that day. Which is... pretty good placement. The real Guernica came out of 1937. German and Italian planes bomb a Basque town for hours. Picasso gets the news and starts painting. Horse screaming. Mother with a dead child. That bare bulb staring down at everybody. Just panic, basically. Then 2003 comes around. The United States is making its case for invading Iraq. Colin Powell is about to give his big presentation at the UN. And, okay, here's where it gets interesting. There's a big blue curtain hanging over Guernica. Completely covered. Official explanation? Better background for television. That was the story. But diplomats were already pointing out the obvious problem. It's a little awkward to stand there talking about bombing a country with women and children screaming behind your head. Everybody saw it. The case for war out front. Guernica behind a curtain. They didn't have to argue with the painting. They just pulled a sheet over its face.

title: SELF-PORTRAIT I
transcript: He went to Paris for a short trip. That was late 1936. Spain had just gone to war with itself. He wouldn’t return for nearly four years. Miró. Barcelona guy. Known by then for the stars and suns and little creatures he’d been painting. Now he’s stuck in Paris. And he decides to do something, in his words, “absolutely different.” He gets a magnifying mirror. Makes his face look up to three times its size. And starts drawing. October to March. Half a year on just one face. Now look at it. Get close, because it’s barely painted. Mostly pencil, with a little color worked in. A giant ghost of a head. Start with the eyes. Two rings, with rays coming off them. Burning planets. Then the shoulders. A star on each one. And up in the hair, those curls turn into flames. He stared into a mirror for half a year, and a sky came back. This is Self-Portrait I. He considered it one of the most important things he’d ever made. And he had a copy drawn. He leaves that copy behind when he flees France during the war. Years later, back in Spain, he finds it in a box. And paints another self-portrait right over the copy. Thick black strokes. Nothing like the careful pencil underneath. On the back, both dates. 1937–38. And 1960. Two self-portraits. One on top of the other. The one in front of you is the face underneath.

title: WOMAN WITH A MANDOLIN
transcript: All right, start with her face. At first, the woman and the chair are one flat black shape. But get closer. The profile, the eye, the lines running down her dress. They look drawn. One thin pale line running through all that black. That line has a history. A few years earlier, Braque had started painting slabs of plaster black and cutting white lines into them. He got the idea from ancient Greek vases in the Louvre. Dark ground, pale line. Here he brings the same trick into oil. She looks scratched out of the dark. Now the room. Green on green. Pattern on pattern. A mirror up top with its own little still life living inside it. Basically a Matisse with the lights turned off. There's sheet music on the stand, more on the table. Get close and try to read it. You can't. The notes are just little dashes. Even the mandolin is nearly gone, black on black in her lap, barely an outline. The warmest thing in the whole painting is a little yellow caught in her hair. Then you notice what he wrote in the corner. 1937. That April, German and Italian planes spend an afternoon bombing a Basque town called Guernica. Market day, streets full. Three quarters of it gone. Nobody could agree how many died. Picasso takes that afternoon and paints it the size of a wall. Everybody knows that one. Braque, same city, same year, paints this. A woman holding still. A dark room. Music with the sound off. He already knew what a war could do to a head. In the last one, shrapnel from a shell tore into his skull. He was left for dead on the battlefield. A surgeon cut a hole in his head to relieve the pressure, and he didn't wake up for two days. He never said what happened next had anything to do with that. But the following year, his still lifes begin to change. Same dark rooms. Same tables. One new thing sitting on them. A skull. It doesn't leave for years.

title: FULANG-CHANG AND I
transcript: It came with a mirror. Same frame. Same paint job. Nothing in it but the room. And the mirror is bigger than the painting. In the painting, it's Kahlo and a spider monkey named Fulang-Chang. Her pet. Which, as pets go, is hard to beat. A pink ribbon runs from her neck to his. He's looking straight out. She isn't, quite. Neither of them doing anything. She painted the portrait first. The mirror came later, when she decided to give the portrait to a friend. Mary Sklar. A New Yorker she'd met in Mexico. Mary had already bought a different painting at Frida's New York show. So Frida gave her this one. On the house. Then she added the mirror. The idea, she told Mary, was that now they could always be together. Frida in the painting. Mary in the mirror. That was the plan. Now it's whoever's standing there. And the mirror didn't come out of nowhere. After a bus crash, Frida began painting in bed, with a mirror fixed to the canopy above her. Lying there, looking up at herself. That's where the self-portraits start. People kept filing her with the Surrealists. The dream painters. The year before she died, she told Time magazine: "I never painted dreams. I painted my own reality." And she lived surrounded by mirrors. One on the wardrobe. One at the dressing table. One set into the stucco of the patio wall. And the one she gave away. Giving friends self-portraits was normal for her. The mirror wasn't. Mary kept the portrait and the mirror together for the rest of her life. Then she left them here.

title: CONSTRUCTION IN WHITE AND BLACK
transcript: It's built like a wall. White blocks, each shaded down one side so the paint looks like stone sticking out. Black lines between them. A little uneven. Now think of an Inca wall. No mortar. Each stone cut to fit the next. In places, you can't get a sheet of paper between them. Joaquín Torres-García wants those walls in your head when you look at this. He's from Uruguay, but he's spent most of his life away. In Paris, he helps start an artists' group called Circle and Square. Mondrian's in it. So he knows the people making modern art out of lines and rectangles. He's one of them. Then he goes home to Montevideo and turns a map of South America upside down. The continent points up. "Our North is the South," he says. Basically, Paris doesn't get to decide which way is up. Or which rectangles count as modern. The Inca had been fitting shapes together in stone for centuries. Torres-García starts an art group and teaches younger artists to work with what he brought home from Europe and what was already here. Now look at the painting again. The grid he worked with in Paris is here. But those little shadows make the blocks feel heavy. The lines look like joints between stones. He's put both histories in the same wall. At the bottom, he writes AAC. That's his new art group in Montevideo. This looks like it could stand for five hundred years. It's painted on cardboard. Glued to wood.

title: SPIDER
transcript: Ok so wait for somebody to walk past it. There. Did you catch that? One piece lifts, another drops, the whole thing wobbles and then finds itself again. Nobody touched it. And there's no motor in here. All black, top to bottom. Nearly seven feet tall, wider than it is tall, and standing on two bent rods. On the left, one big slab of aluminum hanging low. A rounded triangle. On the right, curved arms, each ending in a black teardrop. Legs, once you've seen it. So that's the trick. One heavy thing against a lot of light ones. Which Calder worked out standing in somebody else's studio. Alright, October 1930. Paris. He's at Mondrian's place. Windows on both sides, walls pinned all over with coloured cardboard rectangles. Calder looks around and thinks: all of this should move. Mondrian wanted nothing to do with that idea. So he goes home and does it anyway. Cranks. Little electric motors. Then Duchamp saw them and handed him a word. Mobile. In French that means motion and it means motive, both at once. February 1932. A show in Paris, the motorized ones, and the crowd loved them. One man didn’t. Mondrian told Calder they moved too slowly. So Calder sped them up. Still too slow. So Calder offered to build one especially fast. Mondrian said nope. What he really wanted was for the whole thing to just stay still. Calder eventually gets rid of the motors. But he doesn’t stop the motion. He lets the room run it.

title: NEW YORK MOVIE
transcript: Okay. Hopper fact. When the paintings stopped coming, he went to the movies. And not just one movie. He'd go for a week at a time. Called it a movie binge. His words. So when the guy finally paints a movie theater, you'd figure it's gonna be a love letter to the screen. Nope. First he builds the theater. Fifty-something sketches, four different Broadway palaces. The Palace, the Globe, the Republic, the Strand. Bits from all of them, one movie palace that never existed. Then he shoves the screen to the edge of the canvas. A sliver. Some snowy mountains, half out of frame, playing to a nearly empty house. All that velvet and gold, and the picture's pointed at the usherette. The one person in the building who's paid not to watch. Chin in her hand, flashlight in the other, parked by the stairs with a fat column between her and the whole show. The screen doesn't even light her. She gets a little lamp on the wall, her own private lighting, a few feet from the main event. Everybody else disappears into the movie. She disappears somewhere else. Now. The model for her: Jo. Hopper's wife. A painter herself. 1923, the Brooklyn Museum invites her to show her watercolors, and she talks them into hanging six of Edward's next to hers. Museum buys one of his. First thing he'd sold in ten years. That sale starts everything. After that, she's the model for pretty much every woman he ever paints. Her career goes quiet. His goes huge. So that's who's standing there in the blue uniform, just outside somebody else's spotlight. She knew the pose.

title: GAS
transcript: Okay, this one starts with a car. 1927. Hopper's paintings have finally started to sell, he's forty-four, and the first big thing he does with the money is buy a used Dodge. And the Dodge kind of changes American art. He packs the trunk with paints and easels, Jo rides along, and they turn into road people. Gone for weeks. Cape Cod, Vermont, eventually California, all the way down into Mexico. Half the time he paints right in the car. And somewhere out that windshield he finds his real subject: the in-between stuff. Diners. Motels. The places you pass at sixty miles an hour without a thought. Like a gas station at dusk. He wanted to paint one, drove all over Cape Cod looking, and no real station was right. So he glued this one together out of bits of stations near his house in Truro. The gas station in his head. Which is why it feels like every gas station at dusk you've ever passed. And give it one look on its own terms. The sky's still blue, but the woods have gone black. Night out here doesn't fall, it comes out of the trees. One man in a tie, closing up for nobody. And holding all that dark off, a flying red horse. Greek myth, hired to sell gasoline. So if this feels like a shot from some movie you can't quite place, you've got it backwards. Wim Wenders, the road-movie guy, said Hopper's paintings are like one long movie about America, every canvas the start of a scene. The movies didn't teach Hopper what a lonely gas station looks like. A quiet guy in a used Dodge taught the movies.

title: SELF-PORTRAIT WITH CROPPED HAIR
transcript: So. Frida Kahlo and Diego Rivera get divorced. Ten years of affairs on both sides, and it finally cracks. A few months later, she paints this. A breakup haircut. You know the scene. In a bathroom, at some terrible hour, with whatever scissors are in the drawer. And in the movies, that cut becomes the montage. New hair, new clothes, music comes up, out walks a brand new person. Everybody claps. Frida skips the montage and shoots the scene after. Chair dragged into the middle of the floor. She did the cutting herself. The scissors are still in her hand. She's still kinda holding a hank of it. Nothing's been cleaned up. And the hair won't lie still. It crawls across the floor, winds around the chair legs, one piece hangs off the chair back like it's trying to climb up and reattach. You cut it off. It doesn't go away. Now, the costume: a man's suit, way too big. Maybe his. Because the whole Frida look, the braids, the flowers, the long dresses, that was the look Diego loved. He brought the dresses home from his trips. She kept the earrings, though. The soundtrack is painted right in. Actual sheet music across the top, from a real song: "Look, if I loved you, it was for your hair. Now that you're bald, I don't love you anymore." The meanest track she could find, hung over her own head. And her face gives the camera nothing. No grief, no triumph. Nothing to perform. Because she's not the actress in this scene. She's the director. Then the ending nobody puts on the tote bag: a year later, they remarried. On his birthday. The divorce lasted thirteen months. The painting's still here.

title: UNTITLED (BÉBÉ MARIE)
transcript: Alright, so this one’s a box. About two feet tall. And there’s a little girl in it. So look at her eyes first. Big glass eyes looking right at you through all those twigs. Now picture a house in Queens. One-car garage. On a street called Utopia Parkway. Seriously, that’s the actual name. Inside is Joseph Cornell. Lives with his mom and his disabled brother Robert. It’s about 1941. He’s just left his textile job, and he’s moving the whole art operation off the kitchen table. Down into the basement. So… go down there with him. There’s a little window near ground level. Wooden shelves. Shoeboxes and old cookie tins, painted white. Labels brushed on in dark blue. Over the years, they say things like “Watch parts.” “Marbles.” “Owls.” “Angel hair.” Open them up. You got thimbles, corks, little bells. Feathers. Driftwood. Birds’ nests. He calls it his spare parts department. Old books and postcards piled around it. You can practically smell the room. There’s a story about how the painter Matta comes by to stay, and Cornell welcomes him by opening the fridge, and it’s packed with cake and ice cream. One friend said they all thought of him as a monk. He never left the country. But… he goes into Manhattan. Bookshops, junk shops, dime stores. Comes home with all sorts of stuff. And starts putting them together. Little worlds behind glass. You can look all day. You just can’t get in. Twenty-some years later, Andy Warhol and a couple of the Pop guys come out to see this basement. The boxes are wrapped in newspaper. Then everybody has tea on the porch with his mom. Anyway, come back to this one. Bébé Marie. Early forties. An old doll. Straw hat with flowers on it. Faded dress. And he’s put her in this little forest of twigs, flecked with silver paint. Same kind of stuff that’s sitting on those shelves. Looks like she wandered into the woods in January. Still wearing her flowers. Yeah, it’s creepy. Apparently, the doll was his cousin Ethel’s, and after he died, his family and his estate’s lawyers actually fought over who owned her. And here’s the funny part. Cornell didn’t like what he called the “black magic” of the Surrealists. He wanted to make white magic. Ya know, the nice kind.

title: WILLOWS
transcript: Arthur Dove lived on a boat for nine years. Which sounds nice until you get to the money. He’s broke. He and Helen Torr sail a forty-two-foot boat into Huntington Harbor, out on Long Island, and make it home. She’s a painter too. Everybody calls her Reds. Dove paints what’s around them. Trees, wind, water, the way the light changes. He’s often called the first American to paint a picture of nothing you could name. Though he doesn’t much like the word “abstraction.” There’s no such thing, he says. It’s extraction. And minding your own business. When this museum gets this painting, the press release calls it “abstract or near-abstract.” Keeping its options open. After the boat, Dove spends a few years upstate. The last year, he gets the biggest studio he’s ever had. A whole floor that used to be a roller-skating rink. Then it’s back to the salt water, into a one-room cottage beside a pond. Five hundred square feet. The place used to be a post office and general store. He has a heart attack. There’s kidney disease too, and some days he can’t get out of the house. Reds mostly gives up her own painting to look after him. Now look at this. All those green and gold curves bending over and down. The whole picture seems to droop, like a tree slowly closing around something. The edges are soft and feathery, until you get to that pale shape in the middle. It’s got windows. Two narrow ones, then a window divided into four. One pane’s yellow, as if somebody’s left a light on. There’s a door down at the bottom. Is that their cottage? He doesn’t say. But every spring, he makes a note in his diary. The day the willow outside his window puts out its first leaves.

title: WOMAN DRESSING HER HAIR
transcript: Look at her. She doesn't fit. Room's too small. Arms too long. Ribs showing up where ribs really shouldn't. Even her face can't quite decide which way it's pointing. And all she's doing is fixing her hair. That's it. Which is kind of strange, because this is supposed to be a quiet little subject. Picasso had painted basically the same thing years earlier. Woman braiding her hair. Calm. Heavy. Almost like a statue. That one's somewhere else in this building. Same gesture. Very different day. Because now it's June 1940. Picasso's in Royan, this little town on the French coast. German troops are moving across France. Paris falls that month. And before the month is out, the Germans are in Royan too. So the quiet little hair-fixing scene comes out like this. Twisted. Cornered. Stuck in a room that's too small for her. And here's another thing. In the drawings leading up to this, Picasso keeps going back and forth between her and a human skull. Woman fixing her hair. Skull. Back to the woman. So death is kind of sitting there beside the whole thing before he even gets to the final painting. And then Picasso keeps it. Seventeen years. Never says why. She's doing the most ordinary thing there is. And somehow it comes out looking like the world outside just got into the room.

title: GARDEN IN SOCHI
transcript: Your brain is going to start naming things. Bird. Face. Boot. Maybe a fish. Don't get attached. Nothing stays put. The painting is called Garden in Sochi. Gorky painted it three times. Small problem: he'd never been to Sochi. He wasn't Russian either. He was born Vosdanig Adoian, in an Armenian village called Khorkom. Arshile Gorky was a name he made up in America. He also told people he was related to Maxim Gorky, the Russian writer. He wasn't. And Maxim Gorky wasn't even Maxim Gorky's real name. So everybody's making things up. Gorky means bitter, by the way. That part stuck. When he was a teenager, the Armenian Genocide drove his family out. A few years later his mother died of starvation. He said she died in his arms. He came to America and never saw Khorkom again. So this garden in Sochi is his father's, back home. He just gave it a Russian address. Then MoMA asked what was actually in the painting. Gorky wrote it all down. Old apple trees that had retired from giving fruit. Wild carrots. Porcupines nesting in the shade. A blue rock half buried in the dirt, where village women rubbed their breasts against it to make a wish. A holy tree hung with strips of cloth torn from people's clothes. He called it the Garden of Wish Fulfillment. None of that is Sochi. That's Khorkom. Now look again. That big dark blue thing in the middle? Maybe that's the rock. Those red and yellow bits on the left? Maybe the tree. He never tells you. But once you hear the story, good luck not seeing it. That's why nothing stays put. He's not painting the garden. He's painting what was left of it after twenty-five years in his head. The real place was gone. His mother was gone. There was no trip back. There was only this. So he painted it again. And again. Not because he finally got it right. Because he couldn't leave it alone.

title: NAPOLEON IN THE WILDERNESS
transcript: Find the guy on the left, in the big hat. Arms folded. One foot up on a rock. Keep him in mind. Max Ernst, the Surrealist, is in an old brick factory in the south of France. France is at war with Germany. Ernst is German. Spent four years in the German artillery the last time around. So they lock him up. In a brick oven. Brick dust in his food, he says. In the pores of his skin. A friend writes a letter. He gets out. Then they arrest him again. Leonora Carrington, the painter he lives with, watches them take him away. Eventually, the French release him. Now he’s trying to cross into Spain. According to Ernst, his visa’s expired. The stationmaster takes his passport. Then hands it back and walks him over to two trains. One goes to Spain. One goes back into France. “Be very careful not to take the wrong train.” Ernst takes the wrong train. Ten minutes later, he’s in Spain. Months later, he’s in California, finishing a painting he started in France. This one. The museum later calls it his first painting in America. Look at how he makes it. Wet paint. Press a flat sheet against it. Peel it away. Basically painting by accident. He turns the canvas upside down and does it again. Then looks through the mess for something he recognizes. Remember the guy in the hat? One eye. A snout. Napoleon, Ernst says. On St. Helena. In exile. He wrote that maybe it had to do with how he was feeling, without him knowing it. The tall woman in red is often read as Carrington. They didn’t get out together. Follow the horn she’s holding. Green creature on the end. Teeth. Looking straight at the guy in the hat. Now, about the passport. Before he gets it back, customs makes him open a package of paintings he’s kept aside. It’s full of these blotchy accidents. Thank heavens, he writes. A little exhibition starts up, right there in customs. And the stationmaster says: “Monsieur, I respect talent.”

title: NIGHTHAWKS
transcript: Sad is when somebody admits something. Nobody in here is admitting a thing. Everybody in this diner is doing that very human move where your whole inner life is coming apart, but outwardly you're like, no, no, I'm just having coffee. Look, nobody knows these people. Hopper doesn't give us that. But come on. The guy with his back to us? He said one wrong thing forty minutes ago and has been silently re-editing the sentence ever since. The couple came together. Technically. But she's somewhere else already. He's doing math with the time, trying to prove the night can still be saved. It can't. And the waiter? The waiter knows. That's the job. Refill the coffee. Wipe the counter. Let people not talk. And then Hopper does the killer thing. There's no door. Not hidden. Not subtle. Just no way out. Nobody really arrived, and nobody's leaving. It's not a diner. It's limbo with pecan pie. Now, the timing. Hopper finished this about six weeks after Pearl Harbor. The whole country is suddenly talking about courage and sacrifice, and Hopper paints the hour when you don't feel brave. You just feel awake. The diner was real, sort of. Hopper said it was suggested by a restaurant on Greenwich Avenue, where two streets meet. People have hunted for the spot ever since. Never really found it. And ask him what the painting means, and you get the most Hopper answer on record. Unconsciously, probably, he said, he was painting the loneliness of a large city. Unconsciously. Probably. The man hedged twice in one sentence. It left town fast, though. Finished in January, sold by spring. Three thousand dollars, to the Art Institute of Chicago. Their director reportedly said it was as fine as a Homer. So the most New York painting there is, hangs in Chicago. Which feels right, somehow. Nobody in it is where they want to be either. And if you've ever stayed out ten minutes longer than necessary, just so nobody could ask, "you okay?" then you've been here too.

title: MULTI-USE CHAIR
transcript: Okay, first picture the room. One of the strangest art galleries New York has ever seen. The walls curve. The paintings have no frames. They float off them, on little arms. The lights blink on and off. Every few minutes, a train roars through the room. Opening night, Peggy Guggenheim wears one earring by Tanguy and one by Calder. On purpose. Her way of staying neutral, she said, "between the Surrealists and the abstract crowd." So... somebody had to design this room. His name was Frederick Kiesler. Architect, technically. Philip Johnson later called him the greatest non-building architect of our time. Compliment? Insult? With Kiesler, hard to tell. Legendary ideas. Almost nothing built. Now, a room like this cannot have normal chairs. A normal chair is bossy. It tells you where the front is, where your knees go. Useless in a gallery where even the walls have lost interest in being walls. So Kiesler builds this. Oak and linoleum, curved like a wave. His own description: it curves down, surges up, and falls again. An object without beginning or end. Walk around it. Now tip it over in your head. Once. Again. Every way it lands, it gets a new job. Seat. Table. Stand. Pedestal. Weird little stage. Thing you lean on while pretending you understand things. You don't approach it like a chair. You approach it like a situation. And then the punchline. These things were cheap. Built in a shop in the Bronx for seven dollars apiece. Kiesler counted eighteen uses for one. Seven dollars. Eighteen jobs. A tiny utopian machine you could sit on. Kiesler spent the rest of his life chasing the Endless House. A house with no corners. No beginning. No end. He never got to build it. But look at this thing one more time. Curved. Continuous. No start. No finish. The Endless House never happened. The endless chair is right here. Seven bucks.

title: GREEN TEA
transcript: So Leonora Carrington’s being presented at the royal court in London. Her family’s hoping this ends in a good marriage. Meanwhile, Leonora’s just trying to get through the ceremony. She’s brought a novel. And when she does choose somebody… it’s Max Ernst. By twenty, she’s off to France with him. Famous Surrealist, twenty-six years older and already married. Probably not who the family had in mind. Then the war comes. Ernst is arrested, and she flees to Spain, where she has a breakdown. Her family has her committed against her will to a mental hospital in Santander. They give her Cardiazol, a drug that causes seizures. That’s the treatment. She’s only twenty-three. The story goes that her family sends her old nanny to fetch her, by submarine. Seems like a stretch… but let’s just go with it. Next stop’s another institution in South Africa, but in Lisbon she gives her nurse the slip and walks into the Mexican embassy. In her telling, the ambassador assures her she’s safe. Not even the English can touch her. Then Renato Leduc, a poet and diplomat she knows from Paris, suggests they marry to get her out. So they hitch, and catch a ship to New York. There, she paints this. Look at those clipped hedges, the fountain, that carefully kept lawn. And out front, a woman wrapped in something like cowhide, her arms pinned and her eyes closed. Some people see that as Carrington herself. Farther back, more figures are wrapped in white. Underneath the lawn, there’s bats, eggs, something bundled like a body. And those two animals, a horse and something like a dog. Each has a tree growing out of its tail, chained to the other one’s tree. That same year, she writes on the back of an old painting from Santander: “For you, Renato, in the name of magic, the green which is my color.”

title: BROADWAY BOOGIE WOOGIE
transcript: So, Mondrian ran on a theory. Straight lines only. Up and down, side to side. Red, yellow and blue, held apart by thick black bars. For about twenty years, that’s him. The grid everybody knows. Now look at this one. No black. Anywhere. So what happened? The war chases him to New York. He’s pushing seventy. First night in town, a friend puts on some piano music, out of Black America. The left hand pounds the same pattern, over and over. The right hand goes wherever it wants. Mondrian falls for it on the spot. He goes dancing. Real fancy steps. And he holds his partner way out at arm’s length. Not the easiest guy to dance with. Look at the yellow lines. Chopped into little blocks of red and blue and gray. Run your eye along one. It doesn’t glide. It hops. A writer friend watched him make this one. One day she finds him putting a yellow box into the middle of a red one. She says, but that doesn’t go with your theory. He says, does it work? Steps back. Looks. Yeah, it works. A little later he tells her the paintings always came first. The theory came after. So, now it seems like we’re gonna have to change the theory. Find the red box with the yellow one inside. Up and right of center, between two blues. Only one like it in the whole painting. It’s the last painting he ever finished. The next winter he died, already tearing into another canvas. That spring, a magazine prints what he’d said about this one. There is still too much of the old in it.

title: CONSTELLATION WITH RED OBJECT
