That tracks. People have been explaining this painting ever since. That was his explanation. July 1962. Los Angeles. His first solo painting show. The cans went around the room in a row, sitting on a little shelf. The gallery owner, Irving Blum, explained the shelf pretty simply: "Cans sit on shelves." Then a gallery down the street stacked actual Campbell's cans in its window. DO NOT BE MISLED. GET THE ORIGINAL. Two for 33 cents. Five paintings sold. Dennis Hopper bought one. Then Blum looked at the wall and decided the whole thing should stay together. So he called everybody back. Even Hopper. Got the paintings back and bought all thirty-two from Warhol himself. A thousand dollars. Paid in installments. That set is this wall. Count them.

title: CHILD WITH A TOY HAND GRENADE IN CENTRAL PARK, N.Y.C.
transcript: Alright, start with the hand that isn't holding the grenade. Fingers spread. Bent back like a claw. That's the hand everybody remembers. Then the face. Eyes too wide. Mouth pulled back from his teeth. And the grenade is just hanging there at his side. Small. Loose in his hand. Somehow the calmest thing in the picture. He's seven years old. Alone on a path in Central Park. One strap falling off his shoulder. Socks down around his ankles. And the usual story is that Arbus caught something real leaking out of him. Some little private nightmare. Except the kid has a name. Colin Wood. His dad was Sidney Wood. Won Wimbledon. Which feels like it belongs in a completely different story. But there it is. Colin grew up, and years later a reporter asked him what was happening that afternoon. He said he was copying a face he'd seen in war movies. He loved watching them back then. He was doing a bit. And the rest of the roll pretty much proves it. Frame after frame of a regular kid in the park. Grinning. Goofing around. Showing off. Arbus picked this one. But Colin said something else. She catches me in a moment of exasperation. It's true, I was exasperated. So the famous face is a seven-year-old doing his war-movie act. Which should ruin the picture. It doesn't. Because then he talked about what the rest of his life felt like around then. His parents had divorced. There was, he said, a general feeling of loneliness. A sense of being abandoned. I was just exploding.

title: GOLD MARILYN MONROE
transcript: Alright, so... Uncle Andy needs a hand. It's 1962. Marilyn Monroe has just died, and Andy Warhol is at home making Marilyns. His nephew remembers helping out. Stretching canvases, moving stuff. Her face being printed one after another on canvas rolled out across the parquet floor. But this one gets almost seven feet of gold. One face in the middle. Look how much room the gold gets. Look how little she gets. He just started working with silkscreens. Take a photograph, turn it into a screen, and you can print it again and again. The picture of her he's using was used to sell a movie called Niagara. It's nine years old already. Anyway, Andy used to draw shoes for a living. Magazine ads. Department stores. Actual money. He knew his way around a picture made to sell something. And he knew another kind of picture, too. Warhol grew up Byzantine Catholic, going to church with his mother. All those saints surrounded by gold. People have compared this painting to one of those. Same sort of setting. But ya know... a... slightly different famous face. But look close at her. The turquoise eye shadow doesn't quite stay on the eyelids. The lipstick's a little off too. He painted the colors first, then printed the face over them. So the makeup and Marilyn don't quite meet. By November, this is hanging in his New York show. Philip Johnson, the architect, buys it and gives it to MoMA. The first Warhol they ever took. That same year, Warhol also paints a newspaper front page about a plane crash. No gold on that one. Big headline though: 129 Die. Later, when he's asked about his death paintings, he brings up the Marilyns himself. "I realized that everything I was doing must have been Death."

title: LEDA AND THE SWAN
transcript: There's supposed to be a swan in here. That's what the title says, anyway. Leda and the Swan. It goes... Zeus wants Leda. So, he turns himself into a swan and rapes her. Painters had been painting that story for centuries. A beautiful woman. A beautiful white bird. Lovely feathers. You could almost forget what the bird was doing. Twombly gives you six and a half feet of paint, pencil, and crayon going every which way. Red that could be blood or lipstick. Hearts, too. Which is a strange thing to find in this story. Something over there might be a wing. Just when you think you've found a body, another line goes right through it. You're doing a lot of looking for a painting that already told you who's in it. He's an American. Came up in New York with Rauschenberg and Johns. Then he moved to Rome. While New York went Pop, he went back about two thousand years. Marble gods everywhere. Beautiful old paintings. His lines look more like the stuff people scratched into the walls. But he worked at that. Years earlier, in the Army, he practiced drawing in the dark. On purpose. "My line is childlike but not childish," he said. "It is very difficult to fake." He didn't paint every day. He'd wait. Travel. Read. Copy lines of poetry onto scraps of paper. Until he got, as he put it, into a state. Then he'd go. By this point, mostly with his hands. Paint straight from the tube, or by the fistful. Fingers. Palm. No stopping to reload a brush. All that paint, and still no swan. There's one place where he spells it out. Down in the bottom right. Leda and the Swan. He wrote that on the canvas. Then he scribbled out Swan.

title: PAINTING, 4
transcript: Okay, so he wouldn’t even give it a name. Painting Four. That’s all you get. Most of his paintings, he just left untitled. And he didn’t like “abstract,” either. Vasudeo Gaitonde. Bombay guy. Came up with the painters building modern Indian art after independence, then pretty much went off on his own. Non-objective. That’s what he called it. He wasn’t looking at a tree and making it blurry. There was just no tree to begin with. So have a look. All that olive green, with this dark gray band running across the middle. Almost, like evening’s coming in. Out in the gray, on both sides, these black scratchy marks. Like something on stilts at low tide. A few little bits of yellow and orange in them. Like a couple of windows left on. Then right above the middle, a block of gold. Right below it, a slab of white. He’d use a roller and a painting knife, putting layers on, scraping some back off. You can see the scraped bits up top. He said painting started with silence. And this guy could wait. Months sometimes, before he put any paint down. Five or six paintings a year. This one goes to a New York group show, and straight from the show to MoMA. Then a Rockefeller grant gets him a year in the city. Apparently, the guy running the grant wasn’t too happy. Gaitonde’s spending all his time at the movies. Anyway, twelve years after he dies, one of his sells for more than any Indian painter had ever brought at auction. It was called Untitled… naturally. He wasn’t much of a talker, either. They made a whole documentary about him, and he doesn’t say a single word in it. When MoMA asks him about his work, he writes back that it’s the reflection of nature. And then: “I want to say things in few words.”

title: OOF
transcript: Oof. You know that noise. And Ed Ruscha makes a painting of it. Nearly six feet tall. Oil on canvas. Three yellow letters against dark blue. No fist. Nobody doubled over. Just the noise. He remembered it from the cartoons he read as a kid. Somebody gets punched in the gut. Oof. He said it felt like “almost a patriotic word.” So, Ruscha comes to Los Angeles from Oklahoma City in 1956. Goes to school for commercial art. Design. Typography. How to make somebody look at something. At school, they tell him to let the painting happen. Then he sees a Jasper Johns target in a magazine and decides: whatever he paints, he'll know what it is before he starts. So he settles on a word. Boss. Honk. Smash. Oof. The word is the whole painting. And look at these letters. The curves of those two O's. The straight edges of the F. All that blue around them. Carefully drawn. He knows how to give a grunt the full treatment. You read it in a second. Then you're still looking at it. Two O's and an F. He called these early words "monosyllabic, guttural utterings." Quite a mouthful for "oof." He lent this one to a buddy, who lent it to Tommy Smothers. It fell off Smothers's wall, face down, onto a chessboard. The pieces punched holes in it. Ruscha got it patched up and kept it until 1988, when a group of very rich people chipped in and bought it for MoMA. Here's how he explained the words. You walk into a butcher's. Ask for a pound of bacon. The butcher slams it down on the counter. He said, "It's the slam that I was after."

title: FISSION
transcript: Rows of black dots, neat as a printed page. Then, toward the middle, they get squeezed. Thinner and thinner, until the whole center looks like it's caving in. Keep looking. It flickers. It kinda swarms. Paint isn't supposed to move. But this thing somehow does. So it's the early sixties. Bridget Riley, working in black and white only. A flat board, a grid of dots, and an effect that works on every eyeball that walks past. In 1965, a museum in New York hangs a big show of this stuff. Op art. Paintings that don't move, but somehow won't sit still. The show is called The Responsive Eye. Riley's in it, so she flies over for the opening. And on the ride in from the airport, she passes the shop windows on Madison Avenue. Full of dresses. Printed with her paintings. The show hasn't even opened yet. Nobody asked her. Nobody paid her. My heart sank. Her words. The show opens anyway, and it's a smash. Biggest crowds in that museum's history. One day in April breaks its single-day record. And the dresses keep selling. Macy's. Bloomingdale's. She borrows a lawyer, Barnett Newman's guy, and tries to sue. American law at the time has nothing for a painter whose picture ends up on a dress. Nothing happens. The knockoffs proved her right in the worst way. The effect works on anything. A board. A dress. Which is a problem, if you want it to be art. Riley figured it would take at least twenty years before anyone looked at her paintings seriously again. One more thing about that museum in New York. The one that hung the show, packed in the crowds, lit the fuse. You're standing in it.

title: FRIENDSHIP
transcript: "If you wake up in the morning and you feel very happy about nothing. No cause. That's what I paint about." That's Agnes Martin. Born on a farm in Saskatchewan. Said it was so flat you could see the curves of the earth. When she's forty-five, a dealer buys enough of her paintings to get her to New York. Six years later, she makes this. Look at it. A six-foot square of gold leaf, laid over red oil paint. One of only three gold ones she made. She let the gold dry a day or so. Then she scratched a grid into it. Line by line. Hundreds of little rectangles, by hand. Look along the lines. Little flecks of red showing through. And nothing's quite straight. By now, a grid on a square canvas is her trademark. It's what people mean when they say an Agnes Martin. She'd sit in a chair and wait. Sometimes for weeks. Until a tiny picture of the painting showed up in her head. Then she'd use long division to scale it up. So, the vision arrives. But you still gotta do the math. She said, "I paint about emotions, not about lines." So look at the gold again. Your eye keeps hunting for something in there. The grid, the red flecks, the wobble. Doesn't sound like much when you say it. But just keep looking. Then, 1967. She burns all the art in her studio, buys a pickup and a trailer, and drives. A year and a half. She ends up on a mesa in New Mexico, twenty miles from the highway. Builds herself a house out of adobe bricks. Makes the bricks too. No electricity. No phone. No neighbors. A world without objects. Without interruption. She doesn't pick up a paintbrush again for seven years.

title: DROWNING GIRL
transcript: Brad. A tremendous name for somebody you absolutely refuse to call while going under. I'd rather sink than call Brad for help. You have to respect the commitment. Not to survival. To the bit. Now. Where she comes from. A DC romance comic. Secret Hearts, issue eighty-three, November 1962. Three of Lichtenstein's edits tell the whole story. One. In the original, the boyfriend is right there in the background, hanging onto a capsized boat. Lichtenstein cropped him out. Kept the drowning. Cut the rescue. In the comic, this is one moment in a story. Turn the page and something happens next. Here, there is no next. No boat. No boyfriend. No way out. Just her, the wave, and that one enormous feeling. Two. The boyfriend wasn't called Brad. He was called Mal. Lichtenstein wanted a heroic name. His words. Three. The original line was, I don't care if I have a cramp. He cut the cramp. Then he blew the panel up to nearly six feet square and painted it to look mechanically printed. Maximum feeling, delivered with no visible feeling in the paint. Look at her. The wave is going wild and the hair stays perfect. Perfect hand. Perfect tear. Perfect drowning. Even her collapse has been art-directed. And still, it works. Because everybody's been in some version of it. Real pain, and ready to go under before showing it to the person causing it. Lichtenstein is enough of a bastard to make it glamorous and pathetic at the same time. A sob story, a punchline, and an ad, all in one frame. The original panel was drawn by a comic-book artist named Tony Abruzzo. Tony, never got a credit.

title: DOGS OF CYTHERA
transcript: Dogs should make a painting feel safe. That's the deal with dogs. Wet nose, dumb happy face, everybody relaxes. So start there, because this painting is called Dogs of Cythera, there are dogs in it, sort of, and it is not relaxing. The bodies hit first. A gray-green fog full of flesh, tumbling over itself, legs where legs shouldn't be. Hunt for a dog and you find one dark muzzle buried in the pile. The rest won't commit. Part pet, part person, all momentum. The island in the title is Aphrodite's. Love island. In 1717, Watteau painted it as silk and music, elegant lovers floating off to paradise. Then Baudelaire got there. In his version, the traveler reaches the island and finds a hanged man rotting on a gallows. Birds are already working on him. Underneath, something circles. Baudelaire won't call them dogs. His word is quadrupeds. Muzzles up, waiting their turn. Same island. The brochure got a rewrite. Tanning had her own messy trip to the island. New York, 1942. Max Ernst comes by her studio. He's picking work for a group show at his wife's gallery. His wife is Peggy Guggenheim. He sees Tanning's self-portrait. Names it Birthday. Then he spots the chessboard. They play. Within a week, he moves in. The show opens with thirty-one women. Guggenheim reportedly says she should have stopped at thirty. They married. He never went home. And somewhere in those years, her painting broke open. "Around 1955," she wrote, "my canvases literally splintered." The crisp haunted hallways were gone. Bodies loosened. Paint loosened. Everything blurred and surged. Her version has no silk. No visible gallows. Just the running. Toward love? Away from it? She never said. And it isn't that she couldn't paint a dog. She lived with a Lhasa Apso named Katchina, who shows up in other paintings huge, furry, unmistakably a dog. When Tanning wanted a dog, you got a dog. These, she wanted running.

title: UNTITLED
transcript: There's a rope hanging from a studio ceiling in Japan. A man grabs it, swings out over a canvas on the floor, and paints with his feet. That's not a warm-up story. That's the method. Kazuo Shiraga worked this way for most of his career. He'd given up brushes. Then his hands. He said they knew too much. The paint sits so thick it casts shadows. Ridges lifting off the canvas. And that big sweeping arc on the right isn't a brushstroke. It's the path of a body. You can read the swing in it. Shiraga would lower himself into the paint and drag his full weight through it. And it wasn't flailing. As a teenager he studied judo and Western painting at once. He practiced by sketching plaster figures caught mid-action. Balance. Weight. Direction. He ran with Gutai. Postwar Japanese artists determined to make something nobody had made before. They didn't want to paint pictures of energy. They wanted energy to make the painting. One artist burst through paper screens. Another sent a remote-control toy car dripping paint across a surface. Shiraga wrestled a pile of mud. Then he found the rope and stayed with it for decades. The rope gives him the swing. It doesn't give him the ridges, the splashes, the skids. The paint pushes back. His feet slip. And after all that, look what came out. It's gorgeous. Almost entirely red, but never one red. Crimson sliding into burgundy, with something like fire underneath. The whole mass barely stays inside the edges. Raw canvas at the corners, like the painting was bigger than what it landed on. Then, bottom left, tiny black characters. His signature, sitting still beside all that churn. Seven years after this one, he took vows at a monastery on Mount Hiei. He never stopped painting. He just signed a different name. Sodō. It means Simple Path.

title: F-111
transcript: So Rosenquist spent his twenties painting billboards. Whiskey. Movies. Faces two stories tall. You know, Times Square stuff. And when you're up there painting one, you're way too close to see the whole thing. You can only see it from the street. So he takes that way of working and makes this. The F-111. The fighter plane America was building while the war in Vietnam kept getting worse. Bright. Shiny. Brand new. And he runs it through everything else America was selling at the time. Cake. Tires. Hair dryers. Spaghetti. The plane goes nose to tail underneath all of it. Eighty-six feet long. Ten feet tall. Wrapping around four walls. So you're basically back on the billboard scaffold. Too close to take the whole thing in. Rosenquist called it a plane flying through flak. Flak, like anti-aircraft fire. Stuff exploding around a plane. The spaghetti? That's flak. His word, not mine. Except none of this stuff is shooting the plane down. It's paying for it. Rosenquist said the little girl under the hair dryer is the pilot. Because the people building the plane had good jobs. Those jobs bought the house. The car. The hair dryer. Their taxes bought the plane. The plane kept the jobs going. So the hair dryer isn't sitting next to the war machine. It's flying it. When this opened at Leo Castelli in 1965, the panels were supposed to be sold separately. A slice of cake here. A slab of bomber there. You know. Something for every room. Rosenquist called that a dark joke. You could buy a piece of a weapons system your taxes had already paid for. Retail twice. Then Robert Scull bought the whole thing. Taxi money. Literally. He owned a fleet of cabs. Probably for the best. This thing does not behave over a couch. It wants the room.

title: POETIC SHELTER
transcript: Alright, so this one sits low. These big, dark, rounded shapes, kind of like lily pads. And that top one comes up. Get down a little and have a look underneath. There’s this tiny dark space. Lygia Clark called it Poetic Shelter. The thing about Clark is, she keeps making something, then she gets suspicious of what she’s just made. She’s Brazilian, and she thinks people have gone numb. Forgotten what it’s like to smell something. What it feels like to get hurt. So just looking isn’t enough for her. She’s making sculptures you fold yourself. Paper you keep cutting until you can’t cut anymore. And she tells this story about a basket. Opens it up, and what gets her is the hole. Most people are looking for what’s inside. But to her, the basket’s the wicker and the hole in the middle. You need both. She calls it the empty-full. Now find that slit near the top. The top piece comes right up through it. Look at its edge. She cut it and lifted it. And now the hole’s got a roof. Another time, she’s in a car accident. Breaks her wrist. They tell her to keep it wrapped in a plastic bag. When the bag comes off, she hangs onto it. Blows it up. Puts a stone on it. A bag of nothing, with something sitting on top. You press, and the stone sinks in. Let go, and the air pushes it back. She said it was like a birth. Years later, she’s putting bags of air on people. In therapy sessions.

title: CURRENT
transcript: Look at this for a second. It won't stay put. Black and white lines, packed edge to edge, all moving together. Then right through the middle, everything buckles. Nothing on this board is moving. You know that. But it doesn't help. In 1965, a curator named William Seitz wrote that in front of this painting your eyes get "bombarded with pure energy." He wrote down what happens next, too. Pink. Gold. Blue. Which would be fine, except there is no color in this painting. Anywhere. Bridget Riley had a name for what she was after. Disturbance. So, okay. How do you make a painting that messes with somebody that badly? Riley could really paint. Which, for Riley, became a problem. She'd trained hard. She had the hand for it. And apparently that started to feel a little too easy. Years later she said: "I gave up painting because I could." Which is a hell of a thing to say when you're a painter. But then she explains it. "I had to find out what I could not do." So she starts taking the hand out of it. One line. Repeat it. Bend it a little. Change the spacing. Again. Again. Until this completely flat, completely still thing starts behaving like it has a pulse. Her goal, her words, was "a field of visual energy." Keep building it until it hits "maximum tension." And then, in '67, she lets color in. The next year, Venice. The Biennale. They give Riley the International Prize. First woman ever to win it. For painting.

title: ARMCHAIR
transcript: It's a portrait. Of his mother's chair. Gunnar Aagaard Andersen called it Portrait of My Mother's Chesterfield. MoMA just calls it Armchair. A Chesterfield is a big leather chair with deep buttons. Arms as high as the back. Very respectable. This one has the arms and the back. After that, things get loose. It looks less upholstered than just spilled. Because it was. In 1964, Andersen goes to a foam factory and pours liquid polyurethane by hand. It swells up and sets. He pours more on top. Then more. There's no frame inside. No mold around it. The padding that usually hides inside a chair is now doing the whole job. Before this, Andersen was a painter. Hard edges. Right angles. Here, if the foam goes sideways, it just goes sideways. He makes about a dozen chairs and sofas before he has to stop. Toxic fumes and the old risk of explosion thing. Andersen had a question: "Why shouldn't applied art be allowed to be ugly?" Applied art. Ya know, things you actually use. Now look at those little holes in the arm. Andersen didn't make those. The foam is turning brittle. Bits of it are falling away. MoMA says it's one of the most fragile objects it owns. An armchair.

title: GARBAGE CAN (POUBELLE)
transcript: Alright, it’s a box of trash. Let’s just get that out of the way. Find the yellow folder in the middle, with the handwriting on it. Dresdner Bank. The handwritten number’s still there. Now look at the newsprint on the right. A piece about three London exhibitions. Bottom left, a slip from an art publisher in Paris. And there’s a sheet dated 1962 from a gallery called Der Spiegel. So you’re looking at an art gallery’s trash. That gallery’s in Cologne. In 1964, Arman takes paper from its wastebasket and puts it into a plexiglass box. Pretty much lets it land where it lands. He calls it Poubelle. French for trash can. Okay, so. He’s putting trash into containers. And then he tries it on a slightly bigger scale. His friend Yves Klein has a show at a small gallery in Paris. He paints the room white and leaves it empty. Calls it The Void. People line up to see an empty room. Two and a half years later, Arman uses the same gallery. Fills it with garbage. You have to stand out on the street and look through the window. Pretty much what you’re doing right now. He calls it Full Up. Even the invitations come in sardine cans. Two days after the opening, he and Klein and a few others get together and sign a declaration. They are the New Realists. The idea is to bring things from everyday life straight into the work. You don’t have to paint the soup can. You can just use the can. Or, in Arman’s case, whatever’s in the trash can. This is one of a hundred boxes made in 1964, each filled with its own jumble of trash. And look at the paper. It’s still getting older in there. So go back to the yellow folder. Somebody decided they were done with it. Threw it out. And here we are, leaning in, trying to read it.

title: BAG PIECE
transcript: We got three photographs. Same night. Same bag on a stage. And every one of them taken from the wrong side. Inside the bag is Yoko Ono. New York, 1965. She calls it Bag Piece. George Maciunas takes the photographs. He's also the guy running Fluxus. Basically, a loose international gang of artists making performances out of things that barely looked like art. A sound. An instruction. Somebody climbing into a bag. George is out front with the camera. Of course he is. That's where the camera goes. And all he gets is a pale lump of cloth against black. The curve along the bottom is the edge of the stage. In two photographs, the bag just sits there. In the third, it shifts. And that's the whole event, as far as the camera knows. Except the bag isn't blind from the inside. "We see the world through it," Ono said. Out front, laundry. In there, a window. So he is photographing a lump. And the lump is looking back at him. He's the one who can't see. That mattered to Ono. Inside the bag, she said, race drops away. Sex. Age. You become "just a spirit or soul." You can talk "soul to soul." Four years later, she takes the bag somewhere with a lot more cameras. March 1969. A press conference at a hotel in Vienna. Ono is inside a bag again. This time John Lennon is in there with her. Her husband of eleven days. The reporters keep asking them to come out. They won't. Somebody asks if there are holes in the bag. "There's a hole to get in and out," Lennon says. That's all they get. Everybody in the room can hear them. Nobody can see them. A room full of reporters. A room full of cameras. Every one of them on the wrong side. They call it "total communication."

title: TOMAHAWK NOLAN
transcript: Car parts. Cut up, bent, crushed, welded. And the longer you look, the less it looks like a wreck. It starts getting elegant on you. Annoyingly elegant. Before John Chamberlain could make a living from this, he worked as a hairdresser. Jerry's Beauty Shop. He was welding metal in a barn and doing hair to pay the bills. He said his first sculptures were hairstyles. Then, sometime in the late fifties, he's renting the painter Larry Rivers's house out in Southampton. There's a rusting 1929 Ford in the yard. So Chamberlain takes the fenders. Lays them down and drives over them with his own car. A few times. Then welds them together with steel rods. That one's called Shortstop. His first sculpture using car parts. That was the landlord's Ford, by the way. And the car parts gave him something else to work with. Color. So when he picks up a piece, he's choosing a shape and a color at the same time. This is Tomahawk Nolan, 1965. Look at what he chose. That big yellow piece on top, pitched like a roof. The blue crumple underneath. The red fold at the bottom. Those folds look almost soft. Like clothes dropped on a chair. Chamberlain said everybody makes sculpture every day. The way you throw a towel over the rack. Or the way you wad up the toilet paper.

title: UNTITLED (FRAGMENT 5)
transcript: Okay, so, get right up close to this one. Look for the brushstrokes. Nothin'. No canvas either. No paint. Ink on clear plastic. Alright, so back up a little. Those black bands go up and over, like a rainbow. Then drop into two big bellies, with a little bump between them. Kind of a mustache. Follow them out to the ends. The stripes squeeze down to almost nothing. Then curl under. Bridget Riley made this. She's a painter from London. One of the big names in Op art. Pictures that mess with your eyes. You stand still. The thing shivers anyway. Her paintings begin with studies. Lots of them. But she sets seven aside. These won't become paintings. She wants them to "remain as fragments of a theme." So she makes prints. Her first serious go at printmaking, and she decides to skip paper. Straight to plastic. "We all wanted the new!" she said. There's just one problem. The fancy print shop in London doesn't know what to do with it. So the job goes to a sign printer. Signs. Part of the attraction was that it wouldn't need glass. Nothing between you and the picture. Now come back to that black. The ink's on the other side. They printed the black first. Then put the white behind it. That smooth surface you've been looking at? You've been looking through it.

title: MOONBIRD
transcript: There's a monster in the garden. Seven and a half feet tall, fourteen hundred pounds of bronze, horns, a beak, little wings out like arms. And somehow, not scary. Kids get it on sight. It has that Miró thing, where it looks like it was invented by a child, an archaeologist, and an alien in the same afternoon. Moonbird. His two favorite things in one body. He drew birds and moons his entire life, over and over, like a private alphabet he never stopped writing. Birds, the way he used them, were the go-betweens. The thing that belongs to the ground and the sky at the same time. And look at the crescent on its head. Moon? Horns? Feathers? Yeah totally. He liked it unanswerable. The size is the trick, though. This thing started small. He modeled the first one in the forties, small enough to sit on a table. Twenty years later he blew it up to monster scale, and it still looks handmade. Still looks like it remembers being a lump of clay somebody squeezed. Most things get serious when they get big. This one just got more itself. And it lives outside. Rain on it. Snow on it. Pigeons, real birds, actual moon at night. A creature out of his head, standing in the weather, holding its own with the real ones.

title: EVERY BUILDING ON THE SUNSET STRIP
transcript: He photographed every building on the Sunset Strip. Not the good ones. Every one. The clubs, the gas stations, the parking lots, the nothing little storefronts nobody’s ever walked into on purpose. Both sides of the street. Then he printed the whole thing as one continuous accordion-fold book, about twenty-five feet long, north side along the top, south side running upside down along the bottom. Twenty-five feet. For a book. About a street. If you’ve never unfolded one of these, or even a reproduction, you should, because it’s one of the funniest objects in American art. You keep pulling and pulling and more Sunset Strip keeps coming and at some point you just start laughing, because it will not end. It’s like a receipt from God. The photos themselves are terrible. No composition. No lighting. No moment. He mounted a camera on a truck and just rolled. Everything’s flat, washed out, a little grey, and half of it is empty lots. It looks like evidence from the world’s most boring crime. Because Ruscha figured out that you don’t have to make America interesting. It’s already unbelievably weird. You just have to be deadpan enough to let it incriminate itself. A taco stand gets the exact same treatment as the Whisky a Go Go. No hierarchy. No favorites. Just: here’s what’s here. Deal with it. Comedy timing applied to architecture. And like all the best deadpan, the longer you hold the face, the funnier it gets. And then the less funny. Because all this bland, ordinary American stuff laid out end to end stops looking like a street and starts looking like some kind of species report filed by someone who’s never been to Earth. Like: this is how they organized themselves. This is what they built. Look how much of it is parking. Ruscha said he wanted to make books that were “ichiban”, number one, the best. About nothing. And it turns out, when you strip every shred of artistic intention from a photograph of a place, what you’re left with is the place itself. Twenty-five feet of Sunset Boulevard. Not one inch of it is trying to impress you. Has anything ever been more L.A. than that?

title: EURASIA SIBERIAN SYMPHONY 1963
transcript: That hare’s on stilts. Legs tied to skinny poles, right down to the floor. Joseph Beuys, a German sculptor, used all this in a performance. In Berlin, back in the sixties. On Halloween. So, for Beuys, the performance was the art. This board is just what got left behind. At this point the Berlin Wall’s got the city split in two. And he’s written Eurasia across the board. Europe and Asia, together. Well, most of it. The felt’s covering the end. Above it, half a cross. The bottom’s missing. And the hare? To Beuys, that’s the animal that can make the leap. Get from one side to the other. Now, those triangles. The gray one’s felt. The yellow one’s fat. He says they’re about spiritual warmth. Thinks of himself as a kind of shaman. And his explanation starts with a plane crash. Okay, so during the war, he’s in the back of a German dive bomber over Crimea. It crashes. The pilot dies. Beuys says Tatars find him in the snow. He says he’s unconscious for twelve days. They cover him in fat, wrap him in felt. Warm him up. Keep the heat in. Except, the military records put him in a German field hospital the day after the crash. So, look at the fat and felt again.

title: GIANT SOFT FAN
transcript: It hangs from the ceiling on chains. Ten feet of black vinyl, and every part of it has given up. Four blades. Fat and rounded, like cartoon shoe soles. The two pointing sideways droop like a dog's ears. This is Giant Soft Fan, made in 1966 and '67. Basically, Oldenburg took a tabletop fan, made it ten feet tall, and stuffed it with foam. White stitches run up the traffic-cone base. One cord coils, ending in a plug the size of a basketball. Oldenburg had a rule. "I begin by removing the function of the thing." So he made a fan that can't fan. It looks ready to work. It never will. It went into America's pavilion at the 1967 World's Fair in Montreal. A giant American fan that couldn't cool anybody. He had drawn the idea once before. A giant fan on Staten Island, blowing a breeze up the bay. That one was for an architecture magazine. Two years later, he draws the fan again. This time, he puts it on Liberty Island. Right where the Statue of Liberty stands. Not beside her. Instead of her. He had an explanation. New York gets hot. A steady breeze for lower Manhattan. At least, that was one version. Sure. Put a giant fan where the Statue of Liberty is, at the front door to the country, and you hear the other joke. Is it welcoming people in? Or blowing them back out? Oldenburg said the fan could be an image of America. But he hadn't drawn a conclusion. He'd been born in Sweden and raised here. Either way, this one isn't blowing anybody anywhere. Look at the plug. The prongs are wood.

title: IDENTICAL TWINS, ROSELLE, N.J.
transcript: So, the phone rings in a house in Roselle, New Jersey. It's 1972, the way Bob Wade remembers it. Somebody on the line tells him his twin daughters are on the cover of the Village Voice. He tells his wife: "I didn't sign anything." She says: "Uh, I did." That's how the family finds out. A few winters earlier, there'd been a Christmas party. A twins club at the Knights of Columbus hall in town. And a woman with a camera, who stood the Wade girls against a wall outside. Shoulder to shoulder, in matching corduroy dresses their mother had sewn. The woman was Diane Arbus. You've seen what she got. Same headbands. Same collars. Same haircut. Everything matches until you get to their faces. Cathleen's on the left, her mouth pulling down. Colleen's on the right, almost smiling. There's chocolate cake in the creases of their lips. You can barely see it. It's there. MoMA bought a print in 1967. Five years later, the photograph went on the cover of Arbus's book. Then the movies got it. The girls in the hallway in The Shining are usually traced back to this picture. The family's review was different. We thought it was the worst likeness of the twins we'd ever seen. That's Bob, decades later, whispering in front of the photograph at a museum. Baffled, he said, that Arbus had made them look ghostly. Ask the sisters what they remember about that afternoon. Nothing. Not the camera. Not the cake. The dresses they remember. The dresses they kept. Our mother made them, Cathleen said. They look black in the photograph. They're actually green.

title: CUBIC-MODULAR WALL STRUCTURE, BLACK
transcript: So, most of this artwork belongs to the wall. Seriously. Twenty-five squares of plain white wall. LeWitt just put black wood around them and said, okay, look at these now. The title is Cubic-Modular Wall Structure, Black. Which makes it sound like industrial shelving. And, honestly, it kind of looks like industrial shelving. Except it's hanging where a painting should be. No picture. No center. Nothing hiding in the middle. Just twenty-five holes. Okay, so, LeWitt loved the cube because the cube brought almost nothing with it. A triangle points. A circle rolls. A cube just sits there. No tragedy. No sex. He called it "relatively uninteresting." "Relatively." Even LeWitt didn't want to be rude to the cube. But boring was useful. A dramatic shape can boss the whole work around. A cube can be one cube, then five, then twenty-five, then five hundred. He called it a "grammatical device." Which is a fancy way of saying it was a word he could keep making sentences with. Anyway. Look at it straight on. Twenty-five white squares. Now, step to the side. It sticks out about nine inches. The black strips get thicker. Shadows show up. The holes start closing. Move again and suddenly the wall disappears and the wood takes over. This thing with supposedly nothing going on can't stop changing. Oh, and, before LeWitt was "Sol LeWitt," he worked right here at MoMA. Book counter. Then the night desk. Dan Flavin worked here. Robert Ryman. Robert Mangold. Basically half a future art-history textbook, punching a clock.

title: AMERICAN PEOPLE SERIES #20: DIE
transcript: The elevator opened straight into the gallery. 57th Street. Four blocks north of here. A woman stepped out, saw what was waiting on the far wall, and yelped. Then she got right back in. This is what she saw. The clothes are the first thing. White shirts. A tie. Office dresses. Good shoes. These aren't monsters from somewhere else. These are people who were at work an hour ago. And now they're tearing each other apart. Twelve feet across. Bodies packed to both edges, nobody with any room. Everyone's eyes too wide. A knife up in the corner. A gun just below it. And the blood lands on everybody. Black and white. Attacking and running. All of them spattered the same. Look at the floor. Grey squares. A tidy grid. The violence isn't breaking in from outside. It's happening on the nice clean tile. Then, low down near the middle, two children. One Black, one white, holding onto each other. Ringgold said they were trying to help each other out. Back at the opening, hundreds of people stayed. Her family. Her friends. Romare Bearden was there. Somebody put on Motown. And the children danced beneath the painting. Faith Ringgold painted this in 1967, the summer Newark burned, and then Detroit. She said she wanted to show what the fights were really about. Race and class. And nobody left out. Her own studio was too small, so she painted it in the empty gallery where it would hang. She'd been coming to this museum over and over to study one painting. Guernica. Picasso's mural of a bombed town. So she made her own. Not Spain. Here. She said the painting terrified her. She saw it as a prophecy. Nobody bought it. In 1969, Ringgold and the artist Tom Lloyd wrote to MoMA's director asking for a Martin Luther King Wing for Black and Puerto Rican art. They never got the wing. In 2016, MoMA bought the painting. From her. She'd kept it since those elevator doors opened.

title: WRAPPED ROSES
transcript: The roses are fake. Let's start there. Plastic flowers, wrapped in plastic, tied with plastic string. Nobody needs to change the water. Christo made this in 1968. Called it Wrapped Roses. He was pretty direct about titles. And here's what else he wanted to wrap that year. This place. The Museum of Modern Art. Seventy thousand square feet of canvas, thousands of feet of rope. Plastic over the sculpture garden. He had drawings. He had models. He was serious. The fire department wouldn't go for it. Neither would the police. The insurance people said the minute the wrapping started, the coverage stopped. Permission never came through. So the museum put his plans on display in the lobby. Called the show Christo Wraps the Museum. Ended with: Drawings for a Non-Event. Later, he and Jeanne-Claude, his wife and partner, wrapped a bridge in Paris. The Reichstag, in Berlin. Paid for it all themselves, selling his drawings. No corporate sponsor picking the color. That was the business: sell art someone could take home to make art nobody could take home. But come back to the roses. You can still tell what they are. The plastic lets you see enough. Christo said his work was very literal. He wrapped things, and they stayed recognizable. A chair was still a chair. Roses were still roses. But now there was something else to look at. Normally you take the wrapping off to get to the thing you bought. Here, you'd be undoing the thing you came to see. He made a bunch of these. They went to collectors. And the people who worked for those collectors kept unwrapping the roses. Putting them in vases. Christo thought that was funny.

title: UNTITLED
transcript: Alright, so we've got five green boxes on the floor. Open ones. You can see straight through them. Dark green steel. Four feet tall, filling a ten-foot square. No pedestal. No title. Donald Judd made this in 1968. Or, depending on who you asked, he didn't. Two years earlier, the sculptor Mark di Suvero said that to his face, in public. Judd couldn't qualify as an artist, he said. Because Judd didn't do the work himself. Judd's answer was basically: why should welding count as art more than deciding exactly what gets welded? His metal pieces were being fabricated at Bernstein Brothers, a sheet-metal shop a few blocks from his loft. They did the cutting, bending, and welding. Judd made the decisions. And apparently, this was great for the studio. Before the fabricators, Judd said, it was full of tools, junk, and work getting in the way. Afterward, it got much neater. The metalwork went out. The cactuses moved in. Judd said he mostly sat around making sketches. Before people knew him for boxes, he had been an art critic. More than six hundred reviews and essays. So this was not a man short on opinions. He also started out as a painter. Then he quit. In 1965, he wrote that actual space is intrinsically more powerful and specific than paint on a flat surface. Meaning a real thing in a real room beats a picture of one. So. Stand at the end of the row. The near rectangle is huge. The far one is small. The edges stack up and run away from you. That's Depth. A picture. The thing he quit painting to get away from. And he got all of that out of four identical gaps. Five inches each. Then back to the cactuses.

title: MEASUREMENT ROOM
transcript: People walk in here and do the little museum panic. Wait. Is this it? Yeah. That's it. Mel Bochner measured the room. That's the work. Black tape along the walls and doorways. Numbers at the edges. The width of that opening, stated on the opening. A room wearing its own receipts. Look closely at the numbers. They're not handwritten. They're Letraset. Rub-down transfer lettering, the stuff ad agencies and architects used before computers. A museum room is built to disappear. White walls. Quiet floor. Nothing to look at but the art. The room gets to pretend it isn't in the conversation. Bochner makes it talk. He did it first in Munich, May 1969, at Galerie Heiner Friedrich. MoMA bought it in 1997. But there isn't one Measurement Room they can pull out of storage. Every time it goes up, the room has to be measured again. Fresh tape. Fresh numbers. This version only fits this space. To the inch. And measurement feels like the most innocent thing in the world. Just the facts. Except now the facts are crawling all over the walls. Half the New Yorkers in here are already doing the math on the square footage. Nothing about the room has changed. You just can't stop seeing it. Bochner died in February 2025. He was eighty-four. Later that year, MoMA measured this room again in his memory. Check the gallery number on your way out. Gallery 421 has an official name now. Mel Bochner's Measurement Room.

title: EDGE OF TOWN
transcript: He walked away. Philip Guston was one of the big abstract painters in New York. Soft pinks. Shimmering. Lovely stuff. By the end of the sixties, he couldn't keep doing it. The war. The conventions. His own line: "What kind of man am I, sitting at home, reading magazines, going into frustrated fury about everything, and then going into my studio to adjust a red to a blue?" So look what he painted instead. Two guys in Klan hoods, out for a drive. And this thing's big. Nine feet across. Nearly six and a half feet tall. Start with the car. A black jalopy, no roof, a grey ring hung off one end. The hoods. White, pointed, stitches showing. The hands. Pink, fat, knuckles along the door. Both of them have cigars. Now look at the left edge. That strip of pink, brushed soft. There's a bit of the old Guston. And behind the hoods, the gear. A plank with nails bent through it. A bundle of sticks. Tossed in like beach chairs. It's painted like a comic strip. Nobody's in a hurry. These guys could be running an errand. Guston knew those hoods. Jewish kid, born Goldstein, grew up in Los Angeles. He'd painted them as a teenager. He called them his little bastards. He shows thirty-three paintings in New York. This one's in it. The Times headline: "A Mandarin Pretending to Be a Stumblebum." Meaning: a guy who knows how to paint pretending he doesn't. Hardly anything sold. His best friend stopped speaking to him. Guston went to Rome for a while. Then came home and carried on. Then he says this. "They are self-portraits. I perceive myself as being behind the hood." Him. The Jewish kid. As if he wanted to know what it would be like to be evil.

title: BLACK GIRL'S WINDOW
transcript: So this is the lady who gave Aunt Jemima a rifle. Betye Saar. She takes that little figurine with a broom in one hand and puts a rifle in the other. That’s 1972. The one she’s known for. This is three years earlier. Black Girl’s Window. And it’s an actual old window. Still has the hinges and the latch. She’s making prints when she finds it, and starts wondering how those prints would look inside the panes. Look along the top. Moons, a sun, stars. Things you might see through a window, except she’s put them in the window itself. Then she starts adding other pictures. Little objects. She’s moving from making prints to putting things together. Look at the figure down below. A girl’s silhouette, hands pressed against the glass. All those red and yellow signs across the palms. Moons and stars again. Astrology. They look like hands you’d show a fortune-teller. And watch the eyes when you move a little to the side. They seem to open and close. It’s one of those little pictures that changes with the angle. Like something you’d get as a prize in a cereal box. She calls the whole thing a diary. Stuff that already happened. See those two kids dancing? They’re cut from an old greeting card. Saar says that’s her mother and father. She’s still a little girl when her father gets an infection. The hospital in Pasadena is segregated, so he has to go to the county hospital. He doesn’t survive. She sees those skeletons as his death. Right beside the dancing couple. Her parents together, and then the loss of him. But there’s love in here too. See that eagle with LOVE across its chest? She said, “Love is a bird. It comes and goes. It flies away. It stays.” By the time she makes this, in 1969, her own marriage is ending. The Watts riots were four years earlier. She says both the personal and the political are in here. Now go back to the hands. Those moons and stars from the top row are on the palms too. Remember, she called this a diary. She doesn’t say which hand is which. She just says, “One hand is for what my life will be, and the other hand is what my life really was.”

title: UNTITLED
transcript: Nothing taller than three feet. Doctor's orders. Rothko's just had an aneurysm that nearly killed him. That's a lot to ask of Mark Rothko, you know? The color guy. Those big, soft rectangles, taller than the people looking at them. At first, he does what he's told. Smaller work. On paper. That winter, he and his wife split up. He moves into the studio, a carriage house on East Sixty-Ninth Street. The studio's got a skylight, with a parachute rigged under it. He pulls it back and forth to control the daylight. The doctor said nothing about parachutes. Come spring, he's back on canvas. Making paintings like this. Six and a half feet tall. So much for three feet. And the color guy's down to black and gray. Black on top. Gray underneath. A thin white border around the whole thing. That border's new. This is the last series he'll put on canvas. Now start at the border and work your way in. The black barely moves. The gray underneath won't sit still. Big loops, down on the right. That's not a wrist. That's a whole arm. Find the line between them. Looks like he used a ruler. He didn't. The gray keeps scrubbing up into the black. Rough little strokes, all along that edge. And that white border. It started on the paper. The small stuff. He'd tape down the edges, paint, pull the tape. There's your border. He went back to big. The border came with him. People see the moon in these. It's the year of the moon landing, so, sure. Some see a man near the end. Others see a painter starting over. Less than a year later, some murals he's given to the Tate arrive in London. They get there in the morning. That same morning, back in New York, his assistant finds him in the studio. Rothko had taken his own life. He was sixty-six.

title: UNTITLED
transcript: This is not really a drawing. It's more like a stain his body left behind. Hammons covered his face, hands, and clothes with grease, pressed himself against a board, then dusted the mark with powdered pigment until the print came up. Which sounds ridiculous. Then you look at it. There's his face in profile. His hands together. The body is there and barely there at the same time. Showing up and disappearing in the same gesture. It's 1969. The country outside is protests, police, Vietnam, Black Power. None of that is pictured directly. No crowd. No raised fist. No slogan. Just one Black man pressed flat against a surface. And Hammons is in a room by himself, putting grease on his face. Hammons said he felt a "moral obligation as a Black artist to try to graphically document what I feel socially." This is what that looked like. Not a poster. Not a speech. A body pressed down and lifted off. He kept making these body prints for about ten years, using his own body and sometimes other people's. Here, the hands come together like prayer. It doesn't feel peaceful. It feels like praying when you're not sure anybody's on the other end. In 1969 there was one other place a Black man might be pressed onto paper and kept on file. Ink on the fingers. A card at a booking desk. They called that a print, too.

title: UNTITLED
transcript: Two fluorescent lights. One yellow tube. One pink. You could get these at any hardware store. Four lengths, ten colors. That's what Dan Flavin used. It starts in '63. One plain eight-foot yellow light, on a wall, at a forty-five-degree angle. He calls it the "diagonal of personal ecstasy." Personal ecstasy. Straight off the shelf. Thirty-three years of tubes after that. Light itself as the thing. This one's from '69. Two tubes in a corner, where nobody hangs art. The yellow one faces you. The pink one's turned around. You're looking at the back of the fixture. The screw holes. So the pink never hits you directly. It hits the wall, and comes off the wall. Yellow light, pink light, and where they overlap, kinda orange-ish. Which isn't one of his ten. Flavin wouldn't call these sculptures. He called them situations. The tubes, the walls, the corner. What happens when you put them together. And some people find it almost holy. Two lights from the hardware store, and suddenly a corner feels like a chapel. He'd spent five years in a seminary as a kid, training to be a priest, and left. Now he's making a glowing cross in a corner. But his answer: "It is what it is, and it ain't nothing else." So... let's take him at his word. It's just hardware. He designed more than seven hundred and fifty of these light works. Kept a record of them on index cards. Tubes burn out. He knew that. So when you bought one, you got a certificate. A diagram, the title, his signature. You could bring back the broken fixture, and he'd replace it. You had to hang on to the paper, though.

title: ANONYMOUS SCULPTURE
transcript: Alright, first thing. These two wait for bad weather. Overcast only. No shadows. The camera has to sit halfway up the tower and dead level. Which means ladders. And no people in the frame. Definitely no people. Bernd and Hilla Becher. A married couple in a Volkswagen, driving around coal and steel country. If the sun comes out, no picture. At the beginning, Hilla's the photographer. She trained in Potsdam under a photographer to the Prussian court. So she knows exactly what to do with a gray day. Bernd's the one with the pencil. In 1957, he's drawing an ironworks when the wrecking crew shows up before he's finished. They're working faster than he is. So he gets a camera. Doesn't even like it, according to Hilla. Just snapshots. Something to finish the drawing from later. Now look at the dates on the label. First photograph to last, seven years. So much for the shortcut. Thirty cooling towers. The top four rows are wood. X-braces. Planks. Carpentry, basically. Up in the top right, one has a staircase running up the side and a little window. Nobody on the stairs. Nobody was trying to make sculpture here. An engineer had heat to get rid of. The shape came with the job. Different towns. Different factories. None of these was built to be looked at. Nobody figured a couple in a van would ever line them up. One by itself is a picture of a cooling tower. Put thirty together and you start comparing them like faces. They called it "anonymous sculpture." The last photograph is from 1970. That same year, all thirty are hanging in this building in MoMA's big Conceptual-art show. Called Information. Twenty years later, the Venice Biennale gives the Bechers the Golden Lion. For sculpture. And yeah, half of contemporary photography is still basically living off this move. The grid. The archive. The deadpan style. The whole art-of-looking-like-you're-not-making-art thing. Bottom right. Last one. One smooth curve of concrete. Look at the surface. It's a grid.

title: PATCHWORK QUILT
transcript: In art school, they called him "Petey." After Pieter Bruegel. The old Flemish painter. Peasants eating. Working. Having a party. Bearden loved those pictures. Said he wanted to paint his people the way Bruegel painted his. He's in his fifties when he finds his way into it. With scissors. At first, the collages are small. Mostly black and white. Bits of photographs, cut up and put back together. Then you get to this. Four feet wide. And now he's cutting cloth. Look at her. Pink wrap around her head. One arm reaching out, fingers spread. Legs apart. Almost like she's taking a step. Except she's lying down. He's been looking at Egyptian tomb carvings. You can see it in that flat, sideways pose. But what she's lying on looks like somebody's old bedsheet. And that quilt above her? Actual fabric. Pasted down. Southern quilts were all around him when he was a little boy. Now he's making one. Out of scraps. Find the pink stripe at her waist. Follow it up into the quilt. Same stripe. Then look at her arm. Brown forearm. Gray upper arm. She's pieced together too. MoMA buys the picture right away. The next year, Bearden gets his own show here. Only the second Black artist to have one. And this woman makes the cover. Years later, somebody asks what he was after. He brings up Rousseau's Sleeping Gypsy. The woman asleep, with a lion looking at her. Bearden puts his woman on a Southern quilt. No lion. Plenty of polka dots. He says it's a lady lying down. But he wanted something beyond a nude. Something else. "But I don't know what."

title: SPIRAL JETTY
transcript: Most art fits in a truck. You buy it, crate it, hang it. Robert Smithson needed the trucks to make his. It's 1970. Smithson's in New York, looking for a lake. Preferably a red one. He calls a parks official in Utah about the Great Salt Lake. The guy says the water up at the north end is the color of tomato soup. Smithson says good enough, and goes. He finds his spot out past some dead oil rigs. Several contractors turn him down. Then he gets this guy Bob Phillips, out of Ogden. Phillips keeps telling him he needs engineers, surveys, rules. Smithson's out in the water in hip waders, saying he knows what he's doing. Right at the start, the dump trucks sink into the mud. After six days, they've built a big hook. Smithson thinks it's finished. Two days later, he wants to change it. With most artists, this is where you get out an eraser. Phillips has to run the trucks again. Three more days. Fifteen hundred feet of black rock, coiling counterclockwise into red water. A Spiral Jetty. He's one of the first to make art you have to drive out to, and he's making a film, too. That's what's playing here. On the ground, you can walk all fifteen hundred feet. To see the whole spiral at once, it helps to get off the ground. So he has himself filmed from a helicopter. That little figure running along the rocks toward the middle? That's him. Phillips said Smithson kept using a word he didn't understand. Entropy. Figured if he could get that one word, he might get the guy. In an interview, Smithson gave his own definition. Humpty Dumpty. Basically, he falls off the wall and breaks. You can pick up all the pieces. You're still not getting your egg back. So, there's your answer. Anyway, the lake was low the year he built it. Two years later, the water came up over it. He saw that. He talked about adding rock. Most of the next thirty years, underwater. Back up in 2002, crusted white with salt. He didn't see that part. July 1973. A couple of months after that interview, he's in a small plane over a Texas ranch, looking down at the site of the next one. The plane goes down. He was thirty-five.

title: UNTITLED (PARABOLIC LENS)
transcript: It's eleven thirty at night. Fred Eversley's in the company parking lot. His MG won't start. So he opens the door, sticks a foot out, and starts pushing along the pavement. Forgets about the telephone pole. The door slams shut on his leg. The car rolls down a gully. Thirteen months on crutches. So, Eversley's an engineer. Builds test labs for Gemini and Apollo. His job was to put a piece of spacecraft inside a test chamber. Make it unbelievably loud. And see what comes loose. While he's recovering, a sculptor neighbor offers him a loft. Free rent. Just help out with the sculptures. Anyway, the art takes over. Three years later, he's got a solo show at the Whitney. And this shape comes with him from engineering. The parabola. A curve that gathers things in and focuses them on one spot. He pours colored liquid plastic into a mold. Then spins it. The liquid climbs up the sides. A dish forms in the middle. Physics takes care of that. Getting it this smooth? That's Eversley. Ninety-nine percent of the work is polishing, he said. Now look at what all that polishing gets you. Three feet of glowing space candy. Start at the purple rim. Work your way through the amber. Down into that blue. Whatever's behind it gets pulled into the curve. Even the shadow has color. It's not really a picture of anything. It's more like engineering, aimed at your eyeballs. He wanted to suck people in. He keeps making these for fifty years. This is one of the first. Though he'd tried the spinning part long before the spacecraft. Before the car. Before any of this. As a kid. With a pie pan on a record player.

title: BENNY AND MARY ELLEN ANDREWS
transcript: Alright, start with Benny. He's not posed-relaxed. He's actually relaxed. Like the chair got him before the portrait did. One arm over the back. Legs crossed high. One sneaker thrust straight out at the painter. He remembered sitting for Alice Neel. "It was so beguiling. She lulled you. And you can see it in my portrait. I am just lying in that chair," he said. Lulled. What a word. Then Mary Ellen, beside him. Upright. Knees together. Both shoes on the floor. Hand against her cheek. And she never stops looking at Neel. Same room. Same painter. Completely different way of sitting there. And Neel had time to notice. She said it took several sittings. About two hours each. And during those hours, she talked. She waited for a person to fall into the same position again and again. Their "characteristic pose," she called it. Benny kept melting into the chair. Mary Ellen kept returning to this. Neel said what interested her was that "although they're together, they're also separate." Then there are the edges. Top right, down the side. Bare canvas. And a drawn line she never covered up. Dark blue contours running all the way around both bodies. That's the first drawing, sitting inside the finished painting. The painting is five feet tall, and she never filled the room in. She left the drawing. She left the empty canvas. Then, right in the middle, she finished the two of them. This is 1972. Neel is seventy-two. Two years later, the Whitney gives her a retrospective. Her first.

title: NASIELK III
transcript: So, Frank Stella’s on the radio. “What you see is what you see,” he says. The interviewer points out that doesn’t leave much. “I don’t know what else there is.” By then, he’s famous for black stripes. Painted with a house painter’s brush. This museum shows four of those paintings when he’s twenty-three. Black stripes. That’s it. Now look at this. Nine feet of cardboard and felt. Follow that maroon piece down the right. It turns the corner and runs along the bottom. A shelf. Three slats lean into it from the green side. And up top, that dark triangle tips away from the wall. There’s something behind a Stella now. Have a look under the shelf. Red. Orange. A little pink. A couple of years before making this, he’s in a hospital bed after knee surgery. His friend Richard Meier, the architect, brings him a book. Wooden Synagogues. Buildings in little Polish towns. Roofs piled on roofs. Most were destroyed in the war. Stella makes forty-two drawings in that hospital bed. They become a whole series. He says it’s about a culture being wiped out. Each work named for a town in the book. This one’s Nasielsk, north of Warsaw. Though the title’s missing an s. And Nasielsk’s synagogue was already gone before the war. It was falling apart in the eighteen hundreds. They took it down. Built a brick one instead. Almost sixty years before the Nazis arrived. Now go back to that triangle. Could be a roof. Those slats could be rafters. The shelf, a windowsill. Nothing’s changed while you’ve been standing here. Same cardboard. Same felt. “What you see is what you see.”

title: FIERY SUNSET
transcript: Alright… guess how old she was when she painted this. Look at those jumpy marks. Nothing lined up. Blue slapped on every which way. You’re thinking young, right? Nope. Her name’s Alma Thomas. And she’s past eighty. She spent thirty-five years teaching art to junior high kids in Washington. Same classroom, start to finish. The arthritis got so bad she figured that was it. So she retired. Then Howard University offered her a show. But she didn’t want to hang the old stuff. So she’s looking out her living room window, and… here’s how she tells it: “The holly tree! I looked at the tree in the window, and that became my inspiration.” Light, chopped up by the leaves. Her kitchen was her studio. The title says Fiery Sunset, so you figure the orange is the painting. But the orange went on first. Flat, edge to edge. Then the blue came after, in short strokes. So the sunset’s basically whatever orange she didn’t cover. Tight on the left, looser as you go right. The spring before, the Whitney had given her a solo show. The first Black woman they’d ever given one. The New York Times ran the headline: “At 77, She’s Made It to the Whitney.” She was actually eighty. And that year, she said this about growing up in Columbus, Georgia: “One of the things we couldn’t do was go into museums, let alone think of hanging our pictures there. My, times have changed. Just look at me now.”

title: SUN TUNNELS
transcript: So, Nancy Holt has the calculations. An astrophysicist has worked out exactly where the sun should rise and set. She's picked her spot in the Utah desert. The angles are staked out. She waits anyway. Before anybody digs a foundation, she wants to see the sun do it. December, the sun comes up exactly where the math said it would. So, now they can build. Four giant concrete pipes, laid out in an open X. Eighteen feet long, about nine feet across. On paper it sounds like a highway project. It's called Sun Tunnels. Holt was one of the artists who took art out of the gallery and into the desert. What you're watching here is her film of how it got made. And it's a serious job. Steel, concrete, trucks, a crane. At times it looks like they're building something for NASA. Except this thing stays on the ground. You climb inside and watch the planet do the moving. Holt said she wanted to bring the desert back to human scale. So look through one of the tunnels. There's the horizon, with an edge around it. A piece of desert small enough to look at. She gave it a frame you could walk into. At the summer and winter solstices, the tunnels frame the rising and setting sun perfectly. It's basically like four pipes and the sun, keeping an appointment. Then there are the smaller holes. Drilled through the concrete in the patterns of four constellations. Draco. Perseus. Columba. Capricorn. Daylight comes through them and falls across the inside of the tunnel. Spots of light shifting over the curved surface as the hours pass. So. Stars, made out of sunlight. Which is a nice trick. The thing that keeps you from seeing the stars all day is now doing an impression of them. Her film ends with a note. Inside the tunnels, it is cool during the heat of the day. And there is an echo.

title: GREEN VIOLIN (GRÜNE GEIGE)
transcript: Green, all over. Body, neck, pegs, the little scroll at the end. Whoever did this was thorough. Get close. There's a rubber stamp on the front of the body, a circle around a little cross. Fluxus Zone West. That was the crowd. Sixties artists who figured a concert could be a prank, and a prank could be an argument. This violin comes out of one of those concerts. Germany, 1969. Joseph Beuys sits at a piano in a museum. Next to him, a Danish composer named Henning Christiansen, playing a violin he'd painted green himself. He said he wanted it to look impudent and merry. Basically, rude but in a good mood. The whole evening was called Or Should We Change It? A title that sounds like they hadn't finished arguing about it. And this isn't the violin from that night. Five years later, Beuys and Christiansen turned it into an edition. Twenty-four green violins. Every one stamped. Beuys liked copies. Had a name for them, multiples, and a whole theory to go with it. The original stays put. The copies go looking for you. His line: a multiple is like an antenna. Standing somewhere. Staying in touch. He also went around telling people everyone is an artist. Not everyone can play the violin. That wasn't the claim. He meant everybody gets a hand in shaping society. And he wasn't kidding. In 1980, he helped found Germany's Green Party. Not played at the launch. Founded it.

title: UNTITLED
transcript: Alright, start with the blanket. Plaid. Spread out on the wood. Two naked guys on it. Having sex. One’s standing, looking down at the other, who’s stretched out on his back. Behind them, rusted metal. Broken planks. Then the Hudson. Nice that somebody thought to bring a blanket. This is Manhattan’s West Side. Seventies into the eighties. The old abandoned shipping piers. Ya know… people find uses for them. Gay men come to cruise. People lie in the sun. People with nowhere to live find a corner. Some are just kids. The guy with the camera is Alvin Baltrop. From the Bronx. Black. Gay. In ’69, he’s in the Navy, working as a medic. Photographs his shipmates. Sets up a darkroom in the sick bay, using medical trays to develop the pictures. Back in New York, he drives a cab. Finds the piers. Then he gives up the cab, gets a van, takes moving jobs. Work that leaves time for making the pictures. He parks by the river and just stays for days. “To get certain shots,” he said, “I hung from the ceilings of several warehouses utilizing a makeshift harness.” So picture him up there. Just waiting and watching. More than ten years of going back. Thousands of pictures. He makes his own prints. They’re small. And he tries to get them shown. Somebody looks through his portfolio and calls him “a real sewer rat type of person.” Another accuses him of stealing a white photographer’s portfolio. Only two shows in his lifetime. One’s at a gay bar where he works the door. He’s diagnosed with cancer in the late nineties. Dies in 2004 at fifty-five. He leaves thousands of negatives. Mostly pictures he never had the money to print. Four years later, a critic writes about him in Artforum. Then come the exhibitions. The museum collections. In 2019, a retrospective at the Bronx Museum. And here’s a good detail. The fund that pays for this one was started with money from sales of The Family of Man. A photography book from 1955. Babies. Lovers. Old people. Lives from all over the world. The idea is that we all belong to one human family. It sells millions. That money buys MoMA photographs for years. Including this one. Okay, look past them at the river. Baltrop photographed bodies pulled out of that water, too. Cops standing around them. He said he wanted to save “the frightening, mad, unbelievable, violent, and beautiful things” going on out there.

title: UNTITLED FILM STILLS
transcript: These movies don't exist. That's the first thing. Your brain keeps trying to remember the title. Was this Hitchcock? Something Italian, maybe. Black-and-white, emotionally devastating, nobody says what they mean. Nope. Fake. All of it. In 1977, Cindy Sherman was twenty-three and new to New York, answering phones at a downtown gallery called Artists Space. The first six of these were shot at home, in the apartment she shared with the artist Robert Longo. Six photos. One imaginary blonde actress, caught at different points in a career that never existed. Wigs, cheap jackets, a tripod. Sherman handled the costume, lighting, pose, expression, then stepped into the frame. She was the actress, the director, the costume department, hair and makeup. The whole studio, except for the movie. And you know these women instantly. The hitchhiker. The secretary. The woman who just realized she trusted the wrong man forty-five seconds too late. Which is disturbing, because you've never met her. You've met the template. They look exactly like promotional stills. Not the movie, the advertisement for the movie. She printed them at about eight by ten inches, the size of a real studio glossy. Except there's no story. Just the suggestion of one. Your brain finishes it. You write the plot. You invent the danger. You supply the emotional damage. She stopped after three years. Sixty-nine photographs, then out. Didn't run it into the ground. In December 1995, MoMA bought the complete set. At the time, its film archive already held four million real studio stills. Four million photographs from movies that exist. And sixty-nine from movies that don't.

title: FIRST REQUIEM
transcript: Anne Truitt takes three baths that night. Still can't sleep. She's sitting in the middle of the bed, she later writes, "like a frog on a lily pad." All because of an afternoon looking at art. November 1961. She's forty, living in Washington, visiting New York with a friend. They go to the Guggenheim. Down near the bottom of the ramp, she comes around a corner and sees a painting by Barnett Newman. A great stretch of blue. And the word she remembers is "enough." Enough space. Enough color. She hadn't known a painting could give her that. Back in Washington, she goes to the lumber store. Orders some boards. Buys glue, clamps, white house paint. Puts together something that looks like a piece of picket fence. Calls it First. Soon she's making painted wooden boxes. By 1963, she's got a show in New York. Donald Judd, a sculptor who also writes reviews, pans it. A few years later, a critic says she beat the Minimalists to it. If only she'd painted each piece one color. Judd's reply: "If the queen had balls, she would be king." Truitt, meanwhile, is putting up to forty coats of paint on these things. Herself. Sanding between layers. A workshop builds the wooden shapes from her drawings. The surface is her job. All that work, and you can barely see how it was done. Now look at this one. First Requiem. 1977. Eight inches across. More than seven feet tall. Pink. Yellow. Dark red. Black. From here, maybe a very tall paint sample. But walk around it. The sides don't match. There's turquoise you couldn't see before. And down at the bottom, the base is tucked underneath. The column stops just short of the floor. She's worked out how it meets the room, right down to that little gap. Then there's the title. First Requiem. A requiem is music for the dead. Years later, she explained what had drawn her to sculpture in the first place. She'd been trying to write. Getting tangled up in how to deal with time. Then she thought: a sculpture could just stand there. The seasons could pass around it. The light could move around it. You just did.

title: TECHNOLOGY/TRANSFORMATION: WONDER WOMAN
transcript: She keeps spinning. Diana Prince spins, there's a flash of light, and out comes Wonder Woman. Lynda Carter. Boots, bracelets, hair somehow perfect. Then it happens again. And again. By the third time, it's funny. After a few more, it starts to feel a little off. In 1978, Dara Birnbaum gets hold of footage from the Wonder Woman television show and starts chopping. The plot goes. The villain goes. Most of the heroics go. What stays is the thing everybody was waiting for anyway. Spin. Explosion. Superhero. Diana Prince disappears. Wonder Woman shows up. And before she can enjoy it, somebody needs something. Go stop this. Go rescue him. Go save the world. She barely gets the bracelets on before the power gets assigned a job. So Birnbaum yanks her back to the beginning. Spin. Explosion. Superhero. Again. Now you start noticing what a weird little deal television is offering. A flash of light. A new outfit. A perfect body. Done. That's how a woman becomes powerful. It has to look good, happen fast, and be ready for the next episode. Birnbaum repeats the trick until the trick starts looking like a trap. Is Diana controlling the transformation, or is the transformation controlling her? Television in 1978 only goes one way. Into your house. You don't answer it. Video art already existed. Artists had been pointing cameras at themselves for years. But you definitely don't steal television's pictures, cut them up, and send them back. Birnbaum did. Friends inside the industry got her the footage. Birnbaum didn't own a VCR. She cut it on an industrial editing deck. Then she showed the finished video, not in a museum, but in the storefront window of a hair salon in SoHo. A room full of people changing their hair, watching a woman who can't stop changing.

title: DEC. 17, 1979
transcript: December 17, 1979. That’s it. That’s the painting. And the guy who made it won’t let you take his picture. Hardly gives interviews. But for years, his friends get these telegrams. Same thing every time. Just… I AM STILL ALIVE. His name’s On Kawara. Came over from Japan, settled in New York. And he’s one of the first people making art out of… basically, paperwork. A date. What time he got up. A telegram. Now, he sets himself a rule with these paintings. He’s got to finish each one on the day it says. By midnight. If he misses that, he destroys it. And these take a while. He puts on coat after coat, sands each one down, then paints the letters by hand. Look at them. White. Dead center. He does this for almost fifty years. Thousands of paintings, wherever he happens to be. He makes each one its own cardboard box. And often, he lines it with a clipping from that day’s paper. So the news is in there. Just not on the painting. Plenty have a one-line note, too. One day, it’s Monopoly with friends and a lot of spaghetti. Another day, the moon landing. And early on, one just says he’s afraid of these paintings. So what were you doing on December 17, 1979? It was a Monday. Nobody remembers a Monday. He painted this one. Then on Tuesday, he did it again. And when he dies, his official biography is one number. How many days he was alive. 29,771.

title: THE SLEEPERS (LES DORMEURS)
transcript: Sophie Calle doesn't know what to do with her day. So, she follows somebody who's already having one. Think about that for a second. She's back in Paris after seven years away. No job. No friends left. She picks a stranger in the street and goes wherever they go. Takes photographs. Writes things down. They have somewhere to be. Now she does too. She isn't calling this art yet. It's just something to do. Then a friend who's been working all night asks if she can sleep in Calle's bed. You know, a reasonable request. But Calle takes it quite a bit further. She thinks it would be fun to have somebody in the bed all the time. One person gets up, another gets in. Eight-hour shifts. Keep it going for eight days. So she starts asking people. Friends. Strangers. Bakers, who sleep during the day anyway. A babysitter from an agency. Imagine getting that booking. This is The Sleepers. Paris, 1979. She feeds them, photographs them every hour, writes down what happens. There's a tape recorder. And a questionnaire. She says she's afraid of having strangers in her bed. Also afraid of the silence.
